For working investigators — and for those about to be.

section.subtitle: Disclaimer
section.p: This is the last volume in a four-volume course. It assumes you have read Volumes 1 through 3, and it assumes you are looking for work you can be paid for and sign your name to. If you picked this one up first, close it and start with Volume 1. Nothing here will land right without the ladder underneath it.

Every name, domain, e-mail, hash, and dollar figure in this book is fictional. Where a case reads specific it is because specific reads honestly; do not attempt to look any of it up. Where a template quotes a lawyer or a client, the words are a composite drawn from many real engagements, sanded down until nobody real appears.

Jurisdictions differ. The rules of engagement for a working investigator in Kyiv, London, Frankfurt, and San Francisco are not the same rules, and none of them are advice from me. You are responsible for reading your own statute, your own bar's guidance, and, where the answer is not in either, for asking someone whose job it is to know. The book will point at the shape of a rule; where a shape must be filled in with the law of your country, that is your work, not mine.

One more line. The professional standard in this volume is not the standard of the enthusiast in Volume 1. There is no client in Volume 1 — nobody to disappoint, nobody to protect, nobody to invoice, nobody to lose. From here on there is a client, and a counsel, and a subject who deserves the same care you took when nobody was paying. If any of that feels heavy, that is the correct feeling.

p.emphasis: From knowing how to a craft you can be paid for and trusted with.

section.subtitle: Introduction
section.p: A private HR director in a mid-sized company sends a message on a Monday morning. Something about a senior hire is bothering her — she is not sure what. She wants to know, before the offer letter goes out on Friday, whether the person the candidate says he is is the person he actually is. She has a budget. She has a lawyer on speed dial who will read whatever you write. She has a red line she will not cross, and she does not yet know what it is.
That is the moment Volume 4 begins.

In Volumes 1, 2, and 3, most of the work sat between you and the open web. You learned to pull one thread, to weave threads into a person, to read the places nobody meant to leave a thread. The work was between the method and the record. The record kept receipts, the method did the reading, and you did both.

In Volume 4 there is a third party in the room. Sometimes a fourth. There is a client with a legitimate purpose and a lawyer who will act on what you write; there is a subject you must not harm even when the client wishes you would; and there is, more often than it used to be, a counter-investigator on the other side who read the same three books you did and has already closed the doors you would have walked through in 2019. The record is still the record. The method is still the method. What changes is that every finding you produce now leaves your hands and lands somewhere with consequences.
That is the whole shift. The questions you asked yourself in Volumes 1 through 3 were Can I find this? and How sure am I? In Volume 4 the questions are:
• Should I have taken this engagement in the first place?
• What can my client's counsel act on, and what can they not?
• If a court asks in eighteen months where this artefact came from, can I show them?
• If the subject reads what I wrote, does it hold up?
• If a competent target defended against exactly what I did, would I know?
Nothing in Volumes 1 through 3 taught you to answer those. Nothing in Volume 4 will replace what you learned there. This book is what sits on top: the frame around the work that lets the work travel.
section.subtitle: What is different about the tone from here
section.p: The book is a little colder from here on. Less picture this, more the client wrote at 08:17. Less coaching, more the voice of a senior colleague talking to someone who has already been in the field a while. You have earned that voice. It also means the book will not stop and re-explain method that Volumes 1 through 3 taught. If a phrase like ladder / loop / pivot / independent signals / self-link reads strange in this book, that is Volume 1 through 3 calling — and the fix is to go back.
section.subtitle: What has not changed
section.p: Method first, tools second. The ladder — weak / moderate / strong / confirmed — still runs everything, and it is stricter here, not looser, because more people will read your finding than in Volume 1. Every name, domain, and hash in this book is fictional. You still do not touch a login. You still do not conjure evidence into being to help a client who wishes you would.
The rest of what changes, this volume will teach you.
section.subtitle: What sits in the nine chapters
section.p: The arc runs in the order a working engagement runs in. First, the ethics — not preached, discovered — of an investigator who is now paid, and what a client is allowed to buy from you. Then the paperwork that makes an engagement an engagement, not a favour. Then the discipline of provenance — how a finding becomes an artifact a court can look at without wincing. Then the report, which is the whole product the client actually purchased. Then the specific shape of a vetting engagement, because that is where most of you will earn your living. Then how a target defends against exactly what you have been doing. Then the automation you can actually rely on, without the toy-project rot that eats most investigators' scripts by month three. Then the team, because you will not do this alone forever. Then a full engagement from Monday morning to the day the report lands with the client's counsel — with the mess left in.
That is the book. Turn the page.

p.emphasis: Nine chapters, one arc — from the ethics of the working investigator to the closed engagement.

section.subtitle: Structure
section.p: Nine chapters, in the order a real piece of work moves through.

• Chapter 1 — The Working Ethics. Not the ethics of a hobbyist deciding whether to look up an ex. The ethics of an investigator whose next client will ask them to cross a line — and the language you use when you say no without losing the room.

• Chapter 2 — The Scope and the Client. What a scope document is really for, why it is written before the retainer clears and not after, and what to do when the client wants the answer to a different question than the one they asked out loud.

• Chapter 3 — Provenance and Chain-of-Custody. How a URL becomes an artefact. Hashes, timestamps, preservation copies, the log that runs in parallel with the case notes, and the specific reason none of it is optional.

• Chapter 4 — The Decision-Grade Report. The document your client's counsel reads in five minutes and acts on. Ladder in the report. Words counsel will accept, and the words that get findings thrown out. The paragraph that is only your work and the paragraph that is only observation.

• Chapter 5 — Vetting Engagements. The daily bread of most working investigators: pre-hire vetting, due-diligence checks, insider-risk work, executive-protection intake. The legal frames that decide what you can even look at, and the ones that decide what you can put in the report if you do.

• Chapter 6 — Counter-OSINT. How a competent target defends against exactly the methods of Volumes 1 through 3. Read from both sides: what a defender does to close their own perimeter, and what you do when the subject in front of you has already done all of it.

• Chapter 7 — Automation That Does Not Rot. Pipelines, versioning, monitoring, and the discipline of testing your own code. The reason most investigators' scripts are broken by their fourth month, and how to build the ones that are still running in year three.

• Chapter 8 — The Team. Working with counsel. Working with a junior who brought back weak dressed up as strong. Working with a peer reviewer who is going to tell you something you did not want to hear. Working with a partner firm whose OPSEC is not yours.

• Chapter 9 — The Full Professional Engagement. A capstone that runs the length of a real case — from the client's first e-mail on a Monday morning, through two days of scope-writing, one dead end, one conflict-of-interest that surfaced too late, to the final report going to counsel on a Thursday afternoon. Everything from Volumes 1 through 4, in one file, with the mess left in.
section.subtitle: Then the back matter
section.p: An epilogue — The End of the Course — because this is the last volume of the four, and the series closes. Then five appendices that you will reach for after the read: a Professional Toolbox for 2026 (what to use now, what quietly died since Volume 3), a Templates appendix (engagement letter, scope document, retainer language, chain-of-custody form, peer-review checklist — copy-paste ready), Red Lines rewritten for professional context, Take It Back for the working investigator's own perimeter, and a glossary covering every term across the four volumes.
section.subtitle: How to read it
section.p: Straight through, once. Then Chapter 9 again with a highlighter, marking the seams where each earlier chapter shows up in the capstone. Then whichever chapter is the seam you are weakest at — for most readers, that is Chapter 3 or Chapter 4. Every chapter carries a short exercise you can do on yourself without touching anyone else's records.

If you have skipped ahead from Volume 1 or 2, this book will read as heavy. That is not the book, that is the missing scaffolding underneath. Go back — the earlier volumes are quick reads if you have already done the work. Everything in Volume 4 assumes it.

p.emphasis: Loop, ladder, line — plus three new axes: engagement, deliverable, liability.

section.subtitle: Bridge
section.p: Before we start Chapter 1, sit for a page with the shape of what you carry into this volume from the earlier three, and with the three new axes that stack on top of it.
section.subtitle: What you carry in
section.p: Three shapes, from Volumes 1 through 3.

• The loop. One clue, run through exposure → pivot → attribution, back to another exposure. That is the reflex the whole method sits on. In Volume 4 it does not go away. It just now runs inside a scope you signed, on a deliverable someone will read.

• The ladder. Weak / moderate / strong / confirmed — with confirmed still meaning a hard identifier or a self-link, and never a stack of moderate signals. From Volume 4 onward the ladder gets stricter, not looser, because your finding will be read by someone who is not you.

• The line. Method first, tools second. Shape is durable, tool disposable. You already know this in your hands. It matters even more here, because in year three of your career the tools you learned in Volume 1 will be gone, and the shape is what remains.

Add to that: independent signals only count once each. A self-set name and a self-set bio are one source, not two. A quote of a person quoting themselves is one voice, not a chorus. If Volume 2 taught you nothing else, it taught you that.
section.subtitle: What you carry in that most people forget
section.p: Two habits, less mantra but harder to hold.
• Capture before you interpret. URL, UTC, hash, snapshot. If it did not go into the log, it did not happen. Volume 3 introduced the discipline. Volume 4 makes it non-negotiable.

• A finding you cannot un-name is not a finding. In Volume 3 you learned to write could not attribute as a real result. In Volume 4 that phrase is worth money — because the client who paid you for an honest answer would rather have could not attribute than a guess dressed as strong.
section.subtitle: The three new axes
section.p: On top of loop, ladder, and line, three new axes govern the work of this volume. They are not method — the method does not change. They are the frame the method sits in.

• Engagement. A piece of work that is not scoped, priced, signed, and paid-in-part before it starts is not a piece of work — it is a favour, and favours corrupt method. You cannot do decision-grade work for someone whose incentives you do not know. Chapter 2 is where this axis lives, but it colours the whole volume.

• Deliverable. The report is the product. Every finding you develop must be able to travel in a document a counsel will read in five minutes and act on. The ladder in your head has to survive being written down. Chapter 4 is where this axis lives; it colours the way Chapter 3 talks about provenance.

• Liability. Every finding you sign your name to lands with consequences. To a candidate who does not get the job. To a matter where a court will read the file. To your own name if it turns out you got it wrong. In Volumes 1 through 3 the wrong answer was between you and your notebook. Here it is not.
Read those three as an axis you now stand on top of, not a replacement for the ladder. The ladder still runs the finding. The three axes decide whether the finding gets to leave your desk.
section.subtitle: One small change to the language
section.p: The person you look at from here on is not a target — that word carries in from an era when the work was adversarial by default. In this volume they are the subject, and sometimes the candidate, and once in a while, honestly, the client's counterparty. Words shape what a reader thinks you did. Use the ones that describe what actually happened.
section.subtitle: A ladder refresher, in one line
section.p: You are only allowed to write confirmed in a report you will sign if the finding rests on a hard identifier — a self-link, a first-party document, a government-issued number in a record you can point at — and if that identifier is verifiable by the person who reads the report after you. Everything else tops out at strong.
Everything else, from here, is Chapter 1.

p.emphasis: The line you draw before the money moves is the only line that holds.

section.subtitle: Chapter One
section.p: A client writes at 08:17 on a Tuesday. She is the head of HR at a mid-sized logistics firm outside Rotterdam. The offer letter for a new operations director goes out on Friday. She has read your intake sheet and she has one addition: she would like you to also run a light workup on the candidate's wife. Nothing invasive, she writes. Just the socials. "To get a fuller picture of the household." She adds a smiley. She has already sent you a retainer.

You read the message twice. The room does not get louder or quieter. You have been in this room before and you know what happens next, because the shape of it is old. The client is not a bad person. She has a legitimate worry — a senior hire who once got them sideways on a background check — and she is trying to solve it the way non-investigators solve things, by asking for more. She does not know that more is not free. She does not know that the request she just made would, in her own country and yours, cross a line that costs both of you the case and possibly the firm.
You take a breath. You write back within the hour. The reply is short and warm and says no, and it does not moralise. That reply is the whole subject of this chapter.
section.subtitle: The idea: your red line is a contract clause, not a virtue
section.p: Ethics in this work is not a feeling. It is not a personal creed you cultivate between engagements and hope you remember at the right moment. It is a written list of the things you will not do, agreed to in the scope document before the first payment moves, so that when a client asks — and the good ones will ask, honestly, not knowing — the answer is not a debate about your character but a reference to a clause.
That is the principle. Everything else in this chapter follows from it.

p.emphasis: The subject sits in the middle; the concentric rings mark what you may look at, what you may look at only with consent, and what you will not look at for any client at any price.

cite.p: An ethic you have not written down is an ethic your client can talk you out of at 08:17 on a Tuesday.

section.p: The useful mental model is a map with three rings. The inner ring is the subject and their public professional self — what they said in an interview, what they published under their name, what a company they ran filed as a matter of record. That ring is open. The middle ring is the subject's private-adjacent surface — personal accounts they never made public, family, minors, health, sexuality, immigration status, religion — which is closed unless the subject themself has given informed consent in writing for that specific engagement. The outer ring is everyone the subject touches who is not the subject at all — spouse, children, elderly parent, a friend's Instagram, a coworker's tagged photos. That ring is closed for any client, at any price, in any engagement. The rings are not a mood. They are a diagram you keep on the wall.
Four anchor elements of that map, worth naming plainly:
• The subject is what you were hired to look at, and nothing else. Not the household. Not the extended family. Not the friend who shows up in three photos.
• Legitimate purpose is a fact about the client, not a mood you catch from them. They can articulate why they need this, in a sentence a lawyer would nod at, or the engagement is not ready to sign.
• Consent scales down, not up. A candidate who consented to background screening did not consent to a competitive-intelligence dig against their side business.
• Every refusal you can give in a sentence, you should give in a sentence. Long refusals sound like negotiation. Short refusals sound like practice.
section.subtitle: Before you take the case
section.p: Two stop signs, both worth respecting before you countersign a scope.

The first is on the client. A retainer clears in twenty minutes; a bad client can cost you a career. Before the money moves, you want three things visible: a name and a legal entity behind the request (not a personal email address and a first name), a purpose that a competent counsel could restate in one sentence without wincing, and a jurisdiction you can locate on a map. If any of the three is missing, the engagement is not ready. That is not paranoia. It is the same discipline a lawyer applies to a retainer letter, and for the same reason — the file you build ends up in someone's hands, and you should be able to say whose.

The second is on you. Working ethics has a private layer that never appears in a contract: you do not take engagements where your own judgment is compromised. Not the ex. Not the neighbour. Not the person your friend is dating. Not the journalist who wrote a piece you did not like. If a request lights up something personal when you read it, that is data — pass the case to a colleague or decline, and do it before the retainer clears, because after it clears you are working for two masters and one of them is you.
section.subtitle: The method, step by step
section.p: Step 1 — Read the intake with a lawyer's eye, not a friend's. The client's first message is a document, not a conversation. Read it twice. Underline the nouns — the entity asking, the purpose stated, the subject named, the jurisdiction implied. If any of those four is fuzzy, note it and ask before you sign. A warm reply does not make a fuzzy intake clearer; it hides it.

Step 2 — Locate the request on the ring map. Draw the three rings mentally as you read. Everything the client wants — every workup, every "while you're at it" — belongs somewhere on the map. Inner ring is a green light. Middle ring is a written-consent conversation. Outer ring is a refusal, always, and it is easier said now than said later after a follow-up email.

Step 3 — Write your red-line list before you write the scope. Not a general one. This engagement's list. Family members named or unnamed. Minors. Health. Immigration status. Religion. Sexuality. Any tool or tradecraft category that lives outside your written practice — no logins, no impersonation, no paid data brokers whose provenance you cannot show, no purchased breach data. Put the list in the scope document as a clause the client signs. That clause is your Tuesday-morning armour.

Step 4 — Price the refusal into the scope. A red line that costs you money to hold is a red line that will bend. The scope should specify what the fee buys and what it does not, so that the client's "while you're at it" question at 08:17 does not read to either of you as a request for more work at the same price. If the answer costs extra, say so. If the answer is a refusal, name that too.

Try it (2026). This week, before you touch a client file, open a blank page and write your own red-line list. Not a manifesto. A list. Fifteen items or fewer, each in one sentence. Categories of subject you will not look at (family of the subject, minors, medical, immigration, sexuality). Categories of source you will not use (login-required areas of platforms, purchased breach data, impersonation of any kind). Categories of client purpose you will not accept (custody disputes, stalking-adjacent domestic matters, opposition research against non-public figures, anything for a party you cannot verify). Save the file. The next scope document you draft, paste the list in as a clause and adjust for the engagement. You are not writing a philosophy. You are writing armour.

Step 5 — Log the consent, or log the absence of it. Every middle-ring finding — anything that touches the subject's private-adjacent life with their knowledge — needs a paper trail: what they consented to, when, in what form, and for which engagement. No consent log, no middle-ring work. This is not paperwork for its own sake. It is the artefact that lets counsel act on your finding without asking a question you cannot answer six months later.

Step 6 — Refuse in one sentence, in writing, at the moment of the ask. The worst refusals happen three days after the request, when the ask has already curdled into an expectation. When a client crosses into the outer ring, or into the middle ring without the consent to be there, the reply goes out within the hour, it is short, and it is friendly. The letter of it belongs to the scope you both signed. The tone of it belongs to you, and the tone is of course not, and here is what I can do instead.

Step 7 — Keep a refusal log alongside the case log. Not for court. For you. Every declined ask, every reframed request, every case you turned away at intake — one line each. Six months in you will find that the same three shapes of ask come around again, and you will get faster and calmer answering them. A refusal log is how a junior investigator becomes a senior one without waiting a decade.

Step 8 — Deliver only what the scope contains. At the end of the engagement, the deliverable holds the findings that answer the questions the scope authorised. Anything you noticed on the way that was not scoped — a striking pattern in an outer-ring relative's feed, a coincidence about the subject's neighbour — stays in your head. If it is important enough to name, it is important enough for a new scope, priced and signed.

Step 9 — Read your own deliverable as the subject would. Before you send. This is the ethical dress rehearsal. If the subject read this file tomorrow, does every line hold up as a finding they would recognise as fair? Not flattering; fair. If a line makes you flinch on their behalf, it is either wrong or over-reached — cut it, or downrank it, or produce the source that makes it stand.
section.subtitle: A worked case, dead ends and all
section.p: Mariëlle van den Berg — fictional, forty-one, head of HR at a logistics firm in Zwijndrecht outside Rotterdam — has an operations-director candidate named Rasmus Halvorsen, forty-nine, Norwegian national resident in Antwerp, offered position at €195k plus equity, start date the first Monday of April. She has a legitimate purpose (a prior operations hire two years ago misrepresented a certification; the CEO has told her that will not happen again), a stated question (does the candidate's professional history and public conduct match what he claims?), a jurisdiction (Netherlands for the employer, Belgium for the candidate's residence, EU throughout), a signed consent for background review from the candidate himself, and a budget of €4,200. Her ask lands on your intake form clean. You countersign a scope on the Monday. On the Tuesday at 08:17 her follow-up arrives — the wife, the socials, the fuller picture, the smiley, the retainer already cleared.

The dead end that was never open. You do not run the wife. Not for a moment, not for a look, not "just to see if there's anything." The outer ring is closed for any client, at any price. You reply within the hour and reroute the engagement to what the scope actually authorised. The language you use is in the next section; the point here is that the refusal is procedural, not personal — Mariëlle is not being scolded, she is being told which clause of the document you both signed says no.

The public-record dead end. You start where you should, on the inner ring. The Norwegian Brønnøysundregistrene lists Halvorsen as former board member of a shipping company dissolved in 2019, and the register confirms his dates and role — strong on employment history for that period. But the Antwerp Kruispuntbank van Ondernemingen shows a small BVBA registered in his name in 2021 that his CV does not mention. Not a red flag on its face — plenty of consultants keep a personal vehicle for freelance work — but a gap between the record and the claim. You note it and keep going. Moderate as a discrepancy signal; you cannot yet say what it means.

The LinkedIn dead end. His LinkedIn matches his CV to the month. It looks curated. Curated is not a lie, but it is a tell — an experienced hire who has cleaned up his LinkedIn recently was preparing for a job search, which is fine, or was preparing for something else, which you cannot tell from LinkedIn alone. Two of the endorsements come from accounts you cannot verify as real people, and the third comes from a former colleague whose own account was created three months ago. You mark the endorsements as unverifiable and move on. Weak on either direction; a tell, not a finding.

The conference-photo dead end. A logistics conference in Bergen in 2017 has him on the speaker list, and you find a photograph on the conference's own archive that shows him on a panel. The photograph is authentic — you check the EXIF, cross the venue against the printed programme, confirm the panel's other speakers by their own bylines from that week. That gives you a confirmed placement at the event on that date — a self-attested public appearance with independent corroboration. Useful, but small.

The turn. The BVBA in Antwerp had one filing that mentioned a client name — a Belgian freight brokerage. That brokerage's website has an About page that names its "long-standing consulting partner" and links to a bio page. The bio page shows Halvorsen's photograph and confirms — in his own words on a third-party site — three years of consulting work that his CV compresses into a single line labelled independent advisory. Now the discrepancy has a shape. The gap was not fraud; it was compression. He minimised the consulting years on his CV, probably because the ops-director role wanted operational depth and consulting looks softer. That is a real finding, and it belongs in the report.

p.emphasis: A short, honest deliverable — nothing conjured, nothing skipped.

section.p: You send Mariëlle a report the following Thursday. It contains what she paid for and nothing else. The CV compression is written up as a moderate discrepancy with a clear source path, framed as a question her hiring team may want to ask the candidate directly at the reference stage — not as a verdict on his honesty. The board role and the BVBA are strong. The Bergen panel is confirmed. The LinkedIn endorsements are noted as weak and unverifiable and no more. And under a heading called Not in scope — three lines — you record that a household workup was requested and declined, with the clause number from the signed scope. That paragraph is not a scold. It is a receipt. It protects Mariëlle as much as it protects you: if this case ever ends up in a labour dispute, her file shows that she asked her investigator for something and her investigator held the line.
She hires him. The offer letter goes out on Friday. Six months later she calls with a second engagement, and the reason she calls you and not the last firm is the paragraph on the last page.

One more thing worth naming from this case, because it is easy to miss. The refused ask about the wife did not come from a bad instinct on Mariëlle's part. It came from the same worry that made the engagement legitimate in the first place — she had been burned once, and the burn had trained her to reach for more. That is the shape of most outer-ring asks in a vetting practice. They come from clients who are trying to do their jobs well and who do not know that more is not free. Your job when the ask lands is not to teach them ethics. It is to route them cleanly back to what they hired you for, in a sentence that leaves the room open for the next engagement. Mariëlle's second call, six months later, is the receipt on that reply — the ethic paid, on schedule, in the currency the practice runs on.
section.subtitle: A second case: the one that doesn't close
section.p: Three weeks later, a request from a founder of a small consulting firm in Utrecht. He wants a workup on a business associate he is negotiating a partnership with. The purpose is legitimate on the face of it — pre-deal due diligence. The name is real. But on the intake call two things surface. One, the "associate" is his ex-wife's current partner, and the "partnership" is a shell he is standing up to bid on a contract she is also bidding on. Two, halfway through the call he asks whether the workup can include her, "because obviously the partner is her partner and it's the same household." He is friendly about it. He knows what he is doing and he knows you know.

You decline the engagement on the call, before any retainer moves. The red line lit up on the purpose axis, not the method axis — the request is dressed as commercial due diligence and is actually opposition research on a private individual using the partner as a lever. That is not a scope problem you fix with a stricter clause. That is a case you do not take. You end the call warmly, you write nothing down about her, and you make a one-line entry in the refusal log: outer ring, dressed as inner. The mess is the job, not a mistake — and this one closed at intake exactly where it should have.
section.subtitle: On the language of a refusal
section.p: The refusal is a sentence, not a speech. Long refusals sound like the beginning of a negotiation. Short ones sound like practice. Keep four phrasings within reach and adapt as needed.

• That falls outside what the scope authorises. Here is what I can do inside the scope instead. — For any middle-ring or outer-ring ask. It is procedural, it references the document you both signed, and it pivots forward.

• I would need written consent from the person you are asking me to look at before I could touch that surface, and that is not something I would ask you to arrange. — For a middle-ring ask where a consent path technically exists but you do not want the client acquiring it under pressure.
• That is not something I take engagements on, from any client. — For an outer-ring ask you want to close off permanently, so the client understands it is not a negotiation about this engagement.

• Let me put that in a follow-up scope so we can price it and sign it properly. — For a legitimate ask that has drifted outside the current scope. Not every extra request is a red line; some are just new work.

Nowhere in those four sentences is a lecture, a raised voice, or a hint that the client should be ashamed. That absence is deliberate. A client who feels judged closes off; a client who feels professionally routed keeps the room open and often comes back with the next case. The professional is the one who knows where to stop — and a working practice is a sequence of the small refusals that keep that discipline in tune.
section.subtitle: A safe exercise
section.p: Before your next client engagement — before the intake form goes out, before the first email is answered — open a blank document and draft your own red-line list. Not the abstract one you would say out loud at a conference. The one this specific engagement needs. Twelve to fifteen items, each in a single sentence, each specific enough that a client reading them would know exactly what you will not do. Save the file. Paste it into the scope. Then, only then, respond to the client. You are not writing a philosophy; you are drawing the line before anyone stands on it.
section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • Ethics in this work is a written list, not a personal virtue — the client cannot talk you out of a clause.
• The three-ring map — subject public / subject private-adjacent / everyone else — decides what you may look at, with what consent, or never.
• A red-line list belongs in the scope document, priced, before the first payment moves.
• Legitimate purpose is a fact about the client, not a mood; if it cannot be stated in one sentence, the engagement is not ready.
• Consent scales down, not up — a screening consent is not a fishing licence.
• Refuse in one sentence, in writing, at the moment of the ask; long refusals sound like negotiation.
• Keep a refusal log alongside the case log — it is how a junior investigator becomes a senior one on schedule.
• Read your own deliverable as the subject would; if a line makes you flinch on their behalf, it is either wrong or over-reached.
section.subtitle: What comes next

p.emphasis: The next chapter turns from the ethic to the paperwork that carries it — how a scope, a retainer, and a client become an engagement that a court, a counsel, and your own future self can rely on.
Paperwork before pixels — and the two documents that turn a favour into an engagement.

section.subtitle: Chapter Two
section.p: The message lands at 22:41 on a Sunday. A referral from someone you trust, half a paragraph of context, and a sentence you have read a hundred times in slightly different clothes: Can you start Monday? We'll sort the paperwork out after — I need the answer by Wednesday.
You draft two replies. The first says yes, because the referral is a good one and the fee is real and Wednesday is possible. The second says something else. You send the second.

The second reply asks for a twenty-minute call on Monday morning before anything else. It says the paperwork is the work — that the scope, the retainer, the conflict check, and the signed engagement letter are the first four steps of the case, not the wrapper around it. It does not moralise; it does not lecture. It says that in your practice you have never once regretted spending Monday morning on paperwork, and you have several times regretted skipping it.
The client writes back at 07:03 on Monday. Understood. Call at nine.
That is the moment the engagement begins. Not when you open a browser. Not when you type the subject's name into a query. On a phone call, in daylight, with paperwork on the table between you.

p.emphasis: Three edges hold an engagement upright — scope, retainer, conflict check — and if any one of them is missing the whole thing tips over into a favour with a fee attached.

cite.p: A favour with a fee attached is not an engagement; it is a liability with a receipt.

section.p: The anchors of this chapter, one line each.
• Scope. A written description of the question you are being paid to answer, the question you are not being paid to answer, and what the deliverable looks like.
• Retainer. Money the client has already paid before you open a browser. It is not a deposit against the fee; it is the frame that makes the fee possible.
• NDA. Two-way discretion, in writing, so that what you learn stays with the client and what the client tells you stays with you. Standard, unglamorous, non-negotiable. See Appendix B.
• Conflict-of-interest check. A short questionnaire, run before the retainer is quoted, that catches the reason you cannot take this piece of work — or the carve-out that lets you take it cleanly.

• Refusal language. The two or three sentences you use, in writing, when the scope drifts, the conflict surfaces, or the client asks for a step you will not take. Not adversarial. Not apologetic. Professional.
section.subtitle: What the client wants vs what the client needs
section.p: The client tells you what they want in the first two minutes. The thing they need is usually one layer under it, and it is your job to find that layer before you write the scope.

A private HR director wants a background check on a senior candidate. Under that, she needs to know whether the candidate's story about a specific two-year gap in their CV holds up, because her general counsel has already told her that hiring someone whose story does not hold up is a risk she cannot carry into the next audit cycle.

A litigator wants everything you can find on the opposing witness. Under that, she needs three or four load-bearing facts about the witness's pattern of employment that her paralegal can drop into a deposition binder — and she needs them by Friday, in a form counsel can read.

A family office wants a look at a potential business partner. Under that, they need to know whether the partner has ever, in any jurisdiction, been named in a dispute involving misappropriated funds — because their compliance officer will refuse the deal on a bad answer and refuse the deal on a missing answer, and only a clean answer opens the door.

The gap between the want and the need is where the scope is written. Get the want on the intake call. Ask the question behind it. Write the need into the scope in the client's own words. That paragraph is what you will re-read on Wednesday when the case tries to drift.
section.subtitle: The method, step by step
section.p: Step 1 — The intake call. Twenty to forty minutes, on a phone or a video link, never on chat. Chat drops nuance and forges a paper trail nobody wanted. On the call you are looking for three things: the want (the question the client asks out loud), the need (the question behind it), and the decision the answer will feed — a hire, a filing, a deal, a termination. If the client cannot name the decision, the case has not ripened yet and you should say so. Take notes. Send a written recap within two hours.

Step 2 — The question behind the question. On the same call, ask two follow-ups that most clients have never been asked. What answer would make you not go ahead? and What answer would make you go ahead with a caveat? Those two questions surface the client's real threshold, which is what your scope has to line up with. If the client cannot answer either question, the case is not ready and you write that into the recap.

Step 3 — First draft of the scope. A single page, five sections: subject (the person or entity you are looking at), question (the client's need, rewritten in one sentence), out-of-scope (an explicit list of what you will not touch — usually family members, unrelated business ventures, minor children, non-load-bearing prior employers), deliverable (a decision-grade report of a specified length, plus a source log, plus a one-page summary for counsel), and timeline. Write the out-of-scope list before the in-scope list; it is the more important half. Send the draft to the client the same day.

Step 4 — Conflict check, before the retainer. This is the order that matters most and the one most investigators still get backward. Do not send a retainer invoice before you have run the conflict check. Send the client a short questionnaire — five to seven questions, plain English — and read the answers yourself before you price the work. A five-question form saves you from a five-figure mistake. The questions are simple.
• Have you, the client, or any senior officer of your organisation had a personal, family, or financial relationship with the subject in the last ten years?
• Has our firm, to your knowledge, done any prior work for or against the subject or the subject's current or former employer?
• Is the subject represented by counsel in any active matter that involves your organisation? If yes, name the matter and counsel.
• Do you or anyone in your household hold a financial interest — shares, options, board seat, advisory role — in the subject's current employer, or in any entity the subject controls?
• Are you aware of any prior investigation, public or private, into the subject in the last five years? If yes, by whom, and what was the outcome?
• Is there a source — journalist, former colleague, current employee — that you expect us to speak with, and if so, do you have a prior or ongoing relationship with that source?
• Is there anyone else — a spouse, a partner, a co-investor — whose approval this engagement will need, and who has not yet been consulted?

The questionnaire runs the same way for every case. It takes the client fifteen minutes. You read the answers with the same discipline you would read a subject's own footprint — looking for what is missing, what is hedged, what has been answered carefully.

Try it (2026). Draft your own three-tier retainer band on one page, right now — before the next intake call lands. Tier one for a two-day desk-only vetting: an amount that covers your time, your OPSEC costs, and your professional-indemnity slice, quoted as a flat fee. Tier two for a one-week engagement with counsel-facing report: two-and-a-half times tier one, half up front and half on delivery. Tier three for a full multi-week matter with source-work and provenance discipline: five times tier one, structured as a retainer against an hourly rate with a written cap. Write the amounts in the currency you actually invoice in. Post the page above your desk. Do not negotiate below tier one, ever. The band is not a price list; it is the shape of the practice.

Step 5 — Retainer sizing. Three tiers, then a risk multiplier for the specific case. The heuristic is your hourly floor, multiplied by the estimated hours in scope, multiplied by a risk factor of one-point-two to one-point-eight for anything that touches litigation, cross-border sources, or a subject with public-facing counsel. Half the retainer is paid before you open a browser; the other half is billed against on delivery. If the case runs long, you invoice against the second half in tranches, with written approval before each tranche. The retainer is not the fee; it is the trip-wire that tells you and the client that the engagement is real.

Step 6 — Retainer language for pushback. The client will push. Sometimes it is a real cash-flow constraint; more often it is a test. The client says I'll pay when I get the report and you have to have a sentence ready. Yours will differ from mine; here is a template that works, in writing, in the same reply as the retainer invoice:

p.emphasis: Our practice does not begin fieldwork before the retainer clears, for two reasons. It protects the independence of the finding — a report that arrives before payment invites a client to think of the fee as contingent on the answer, and a contingent fee is incompatible with decision-grade work. And it protects the client — we have declined engagements at this stage before, on conflict grounds, and it is cleaner for both parties if that conversation happens now than after work has begun. The retainer is refundable up to the moment we open the first source; after that, it is against work performed.

section.p: That paragraph, adapted to your voice, is worth writing once and keeping in a template. Do not send it in anger; send it in the same tone as the rest of the correspondence. Most clients read it and pay the invoice within the hour. The ones who do not are usually the ones the conflict check would have caught anyway.

Step 7 — Engagement letter and NDA. Standard professional documents, adapted to the jurisdiction you work under and reviewed by your own counsel once, then re-used. The engagement letter names the parties, references the scope document by version and date, states the fee structure, and closes with the boilerplate on liability, indemnity, and governing law that your own lawyer wrote for you. The NDA is two-way. Neither document is exotic. See Appendix B for the template forms — including the specific retainer language above rendered as a clause, and the conflict-check questionnaire rendered as an exhibit.

Step 8 — Sign. Both parties sign the engagement letter and the NDA on the same day the retainer clears. Not before. Not after. All three things — signed letter, signed NDA, cleared retainer — land inside the same twenty-four hours. If any one of the three is missing on the morning you were meant to start, the engagement has not started and you say so, out loud, in writing.

Step 9 — Kick-off. A short written note to the client — one paragraph — confirming that the engagement is live, restating the scope in one sentence, restating the deliverable and the deadline, and naming the single point of contact on each side. That note is the last piece of paperwork before the pixels. Save it. It is the document you will re-read on the day the case tries to change shape.
section.subtitle: A worked case, dead ends and all
section.p: The referral comes on a Sunday night from a lawyer you have worked with twice before. Her sister-in-law runs HR at a mid-sized industrial-controls company — call it Halden Systems, fictional, based in a small city you have never worked in — and Halden has a senior hire in the final round. The candidate, Owen Rask, has a clean CV, a strong reference from a former CEO, and a two-year gap between 2019 and 2021 that he explains as a family-care period. Halden's counsel wants the gap looked at, and one prior employer — a subcontractor called Meridian Field Services — checked against public records. Offer letter goes out on Friday.

You reply Monday morning, book the intake call for ten, and send the conflict-check questionnaire ahead of the call so the client can fill it out in advance. On the call — thirty-eight minutes, notes taken — the want is clear (background on Owen Rask), the need is one layer down (does the family-care story line up, and is there anything about Meridian that would embarrass Halden), and the decision is the Friday offer letter. You ask the two follow-ups. What answer would make you not go ahead? — anything that suggests the gap was actually a departure under a cloud from a fifth employer nobody has mentioned. What answer would make you go ahead with a caveat? — a resolved civil dispute at a prior employer, disclosed and settled. Good answers. The case is ripe. You send the recap by lunch.

Dead end one — the questionnaire comes back thin. The client's completed conflict questionnaire has three questions answered N/A and one answered not sure. The not sure is question two, whether your firm has done prior work for or against the subject's current or former employer. Meridian Field Services rings a faint bell for you — a name half-familiar from a matter in 2024 you cannot immediately place. You do not proceed on not sure. You pull your own engagement log for 2023–2024 and search it by employer name and by counterparty name. It takes forty minutes and turns up a matter from May 2024 in which your firm produced a short due-diligence memo for a private-equity buyer who was, at the time, considering an acquisition of Meridian's parent group. The deal did not close, the memo was thin, and you never spoke to Meridian directly — but you were paid to look at their books, and that is a relationship.

Dead end two — is it disqualifying? You do not know yet, and the correct move is not to guess. You send the client a written note within the hour of finding it: In running our conflict check we identified prior paid work in 2024 involving Meridian's parent group. The scope of that work was narrow, the deal did not close, and we did not develop a client relationship with Meridian itself. We are pausing the intake pending your instructions. Options: proceed with a specific carve-out excluding Meridian from our scope; proceed unrestricted with your written waiver after disclosure; or decline the engagement. We recommend the first. The client forwards the note to her general counsel. The counsel replies four hours later: Understood. We accept option one — carve out Meridian entirely from your scope. We will run the Meridian check ourselves through a different firm. Please re-issue the scope document with the carve-out written in and we will countersign.

Dead end three — the retainer language runs into a policy wall. You re-issue the scope with the carve-out and send the retainer invoice. Halden's finance department writes back that their vendor policy is thirty-day net on all invoices and they cannot pay a retainer up front — a real policy, written down, not a manoeuvre. You have a decision. You send the retainer paragraph from your template, unchanged in tone, and add one sentence: We understand the vendor-onboarding constraint. We are able to structure this engagement under a fixed-fee purchase order rather than a retainer, billed fifty percent at signature and fifty percent at delivery, with the same non-refundable clause after opening the first source. That structure is compatible with your net-thirty terms on the second half. It is not compatible with commencing fieldwork before the first fifty percent has been received. Halden's finance approves the purchase-order structure the next morning. The engagement has moved, and it has not degraded.

Dead end four — a source-conflict question surfaces from the client, not you. Late in the same day, the HR director writes with a small confession. She had wanted to ask a former colleague of Rask's — someone she happens to know socially — for an informal reference. She has not done it yet; she is asking whether she can. You write back: No. Once we are engaged on the vetting, informal outreach by you to someone in the subject's network risks contaminating the record — the person you speak to may then behave differently online, or reach out to Rask directly, and the trail we then find will not be the trail that existed before your call. If we need a reference, we will surface the person through the scope and the client will decide how to approach them, but not casually, and not before we know what the open record shows. She accepts. That paragraph is now part of your standard kick-off note.
By Wednesday morning the engagement letter is signed, the amended scope is countersigned, the fifty-percent tranche has cleared, and the NDA is in the file. The pixels can begin.

section.p: Rank the case on the ladder as it stands at the kick-off, not the answer: the engagement itself is confirmed — you have signed paper on both sides. That is the strongest thing in the file so far. Everything about Owen Rask is still at weak because you have not opened a source. That is exactly the right asymmetry at kick-off, and it is what the paperwork gave you.
section.subtitle: A second case: the one that doesn't close
section.p: Same week, a different intake. A small crypto fund wants a look at a fund manager they are recruiting. The referral is warm; the fee is generous. On the intake call the want is a background on Nils Voss, but the need is unclear — the recruiter cannot name the decision the answer will feed, and cannot answer what answer would make you not go ahead. Yellow flag, not red. You send the conflict-check questionnaire and the retainer invoice. The client refuses the questionnaire — we don't do those; our compliance handles conflicts — and refuses the retainer, offering payment on delivery, whatever the answer. Two red flags in the same reply. You send one polite paragraph declining the engagement. The client walks. You lose the fee and are glad you did — a case with no named decision, no conflict check, and a fee contingent on the answer is not a case; it is a way to end up in an arbitration you did not plan on. Kick-off ladder rank: not applicable. There is no engagement to rank.
section.subtitle: When a conflict surfaces mid-engagement
section.p: Sometimes the conflict is not visible on Monday. It surfaces on Wednesday, when the subject's name shows up in a document from an unrelated matter still open in your firm's file, or when a source you were going to interview turns out to be a former colleague of your co-worker, or when a corporate structure resolves and you find your own client's parent is a shareholder in the subject's employer. The rule is not complicated and it does not bend.
Freeze. Stop opening sources the moment you see it. Do not push through to finish the thought — the thought is now contaminated.

Disclose in writing, the same day. One paragraph to the client, plain language, describing the conflict, the moment you noticed it, and the fact that you have stopped work. Do not speculate about materiality; state facts and ask for instructions.

Offer options. Continue with a written carve-out that excludes the conflicted branch and note it in the report. Hand off the conflicted branch to a partner firm on the client's approval. Or withdraw entirely, refund the unearned portion of the retainer, and hand over your log so the client's next investigator does not repeat the work you already did.

Do not continue on client waiver alone if the conflict is material. A client can waive a conflict that touches their own interests; they cannot waive a conflict that touches the subject's rights or the integrity of the record. If in doubt, withdraw. It is cheaper than the alternative, always, and the referral you preserve by withdrawing well is worth more than the fee you lose.
section.subtitle: A safe exercise
section.p: Before your next intake call — this week, ideally — draft your own conflict-check questionnaire. Five to seven questions, in your own voice, covering employer-history, family-tie, prior-representation, financial-interest, and source-conflict at a minimum. Write it once. Save it as a template. Send it with every intake from now on. The first time it saves you from a case you would have regretted, you will know the exercise paid for itself, and the second time you will stop counting.
section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • Paperwork before pixels: scope, retainer, NDA, conflict check, kick-off note — all four rails before you open a browser.
• The client tells you their want in two minutes; the need is one layer down, and the scope is written to the need.
• Ask the two follow-ups on the intake call: what answer would make you not go ahead, and what answer would let you go ahead with a caveat.
• Run the conflict check before you send the retainer invoice, not after. A five-question form catches a five-figure mistake.
• Retainer sizing lives on a three-tier band with a risk multiplier; do not negotiate below tier one, ever.
• When the client pushes back on the retainer, send the paragraph — the same tone as the rest of the correspondence — and let the invoice do its work.
• Engagement letter and NDA are standard professional documents; the templates are in Appendix B.
• A conflict that surfaces mid-engagement is a freeze-and-disclose event, not a push-through-to-finish event.
• A case with no named decision, no conflict check, and a fee contingent on the answer is not an engagement — decline it in one paragraph.
section.subtitle: What comes next
section.p: The next chapter turns from the paperwork that lets a finding travel to the discipline that lets a finding stand — provenance, hashes, chain-of-custody, and the log that runs in parallel with the case notes.

p.emphasis: An artefact without provenance is a rumour. Provenance is the work you do for the version of yourself who is not in the room.

section.subtitle: Chapter Three
section.p: The e-mail is polite and it is late. The matter you closed eighteen months ago is being reopened, and opposing counsel — a name you do not know, at a firm you do — has a specific question. On page nine of the report you filed with your client's lawyer in early 2025 there is a screenshot of a post from the subject's account, captioned retrieved 12 March 2025, 13:07 UTC. The account is now gone. The post, they say, never existed. Where did you get it. When exactly. How would you show that today.

You do not answer immediately. You do not need to. You open the case folder — the one that lived on an encrypted drive for eighteen months and has not been touched since the invoice cleared — and you open the second file in it. Not the case notes. The log.
Everything you need is on one line.
You do not read the line yet. You close the folder. You go and pour a coffee. Then you write back to counsel and say you will have a full provenance chain to them by end of day tomorrow.
That reflex — the one where you already know the answer is in the log because you know how you work — is the whole of this chapter.
