p.emphasis: A URL becomes an artefact when you fix its form, hash the bytes you fetched, and pin two independent preservation copies against a UTC clock — every step signed into a log that runs alongside your notes, not inside them.

cite.p: Provenance is what turns evidence into something you can be asked about.

section.p: Provenance is not one act. It is five anchor elements, taken in the same order every time, so that eighteen months from now the person who reopens the case — even if that person is you and you have forgotten everything — can walk the chain without ambiguity. The anchors are these:
• The URL, in every plausible form the target used, before you fetch anything.
• The UTC capture time, from a clock you have already checked against a public source that day.
• The SHA-256 of the bytes you actually fetched — the HTML, the JSON, the image, the PDF, whatever left the wire.
• Two independent preservation copies, on two independent archives, taken close in time.
• A one-line intent entry — why you fetched this, in the words of the scope. Not what you found. Why you went looking.
Everything else in this chapter is how those five anchors sit in a log you can defend.
section.subtitle: What died since Volume 3
section.p: Not much, and that is the good news. Google's cache: is still dead and is not coming back; Volume 3 already told you to stop reaching for it, and the muscle memory is by now mostly gone. Perma.cc is still healthy and is still the archive counsel most often knows by name — free at low volume, institutionally hosted, defensible on the stand. archive.today is still the workhorse for single social posts, but it throttles harder in 2026 than it did in 2024 and will occasionally return a soft failure that looks like a success; you now verify every archive.today capture by re-opening its short URL in a clean tab before you close the log line. Wayback is still Wayback — indispensable and imperfect, thin on the walled platforms and thick on the open web.

The real change is smaller and older than the tooling. Discipline has moved forward one step. In Volume 3 you preserved after you found something worth citing. In Volume 4 you preserve before — at the moment you fetch, before you have any idea whether the page will matter. You cannot back-fill a chain of custody. You can only decide, now, to be the investigator who has one.

There is also a small emerging option worth naming and moving past: BLAKE3 is faster than SHA-256 and is showing up in more toolchains, and if your team standardises on it internally that is fine — but for anything that leaves your desk and lands with counsel, SHA-256 is still the hash the reviewer expects to see, and there is no reason to spend the room's attention on a novelty.
section.subtitle: Before you touch the URL
section.p: Three moves, in this order, every time. They are boring and they are non-negotiable.

Use a clean research browser — a profile with no personal cookies, no logged-in Google, no autofill, no extensions that phone home. Sync off. History local. Whatever profile you use for the news is not the profile you use for a subject; the two must not touch. A subject who watches their referrer log or their platform analytics can read a lot from the wrong browser reaching them.

Check your clock against the world. Before the first fetch of the day, run one query against a public NTP source — pool.ntp.org is fine, so is time.nist.gov — and write the offset into the first line of the day's log. If your machine is fifteen seconds off, you want to know at the top of the day, not at the bottom of a deposition. A modern workstation is usually accurate to sub-second; the point is to have written down that you checked.

Decide, before you fetch, what question the fetch is against. One sentence, drawn from the scope. Verifying subject's earlier statement re. contract dated 12 January. If you cannot write that sentence, you are not fetching yet — you are browsing, and browsing does not belong in a case file.
section.subtitle: The method, step by step
section.p: Step 1 — Fix the URL forms. Before you go near the network, write out every plausible form of the URL the subject uses: the canonical (example.com/post/1234), the vanity (example.com/@handle/slug), the mobile subdomain (m.example.com/…), the share URL (example.com/s/aB3xQ), any AMP or reader-mode variant, the deep link to a specific reply, the embed form. Different archives indexed different forms; a chain that resolves on one form and dies on another is a chain with one flat tire.

Step 2 — Fetch and hash. Fetch the artefact into a file. For a page, that is the raw HTML your client actually receives, not a rendered screenshot; for an image or PDF, the file itself; for a JSON endpoint, the JSON payload. Then hash it. On Linux and macOS, shasum -a 256 file. On Windows, Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 file. The hash is a fingerprint of the bytes — if a byte changes, the hash changes. Two people who fetch the same page seconds apart can get different hashes for good reasons (ad rotation, per-session tokens), which is why the hash pins what you fetched, not what the page currently is.

Step 3 — Snapshot to Wayback. Push the URL to the Wayback Machine's Save Page Now: web.archive.org/save/<url>. Wait for the capture to complete. Copy the resulting timestamped URL — the one that looks like web.archive.org/web/20260814130722/…. That timestamp is the capture time in UTC; do not paraphrase it, copy it.

Step 4 — Snapshot to archive.today. In a clean tab, archive.ph/newest/<url> or the site's own save form. Wait for it to render. Verify — this is the step 2026 added — that the short URL it returns actually loads a real page and not the soft-failure "processing" pane. If it failed, take it again. archive.today captures often preserve content Wayback loses on walled platforms; two independent archives is your floor. If the matter is likely to see court, add a third — Perma.cc for a lawyer-facing chain, or a national web archive for the relevant jurisdiction — and note in the log which archive is which.

Step 5 — Record the capture UTC. Not local time. Not "this afternoon." The full ISO-8601 stamp, 2026-08-14T13:07:22Z, from the archive's own response header when you can get it, or from a UTC clock on your own machine — the one you checked in step zero — when you cannot. UTC is the only clock that survives a case reopening across jurisdictions and daylight saving.

Step 6 — Record intent. Write the one-sentence reason for the fetch, in the words of the scope. Verifying subject's earlier statement re. contract dated 12 January. Not interesting post and not looks relevant — a scope-anchored sentence. The intent line is what protects you from the accusation you were fishing, and it protects the subject from the reality that sometimes we were.

Step 7 — Sign the log line. This is the discipline Volume 3 hinted at and Volume 4 requires. Each entry in the log carries a small hash of its own, computed over the entry's contents and the previous entry's signature. It is a lightweight chain: change any line and every signature after it goes wrong. You do not need cryptographic ceremony for this — a shell one-liner that reads the previous signature, appends the new entry, and pipes the whole thing through sha256sum (on Windows, Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256; on macOS, shasum -a 256) is enough. What matters is that the log is not a file you can quietly edit six months later without leaving a trace.

Try it (2026). Pick one URL you fetched in the course of your ordinary work today — a news story, a documentation page, anything that will still exist tomorrow. Hash the file you fetched. Push the URL to Wayback and archive.today. Write the five anchors into a one-line entry, sign it with the SHA-256 of the entry, and close the log. Come back tomorrow and verify: does the hash still match the file, do both archive URLs still resolve, does the log line's signature verify against its contents. That reflex, made routine on nothing that matters, is the reflex that saves you on something that does.

Step 8 — Export the daily log at end of day. A single text file, one line per fetch, in a folder that is backed up and encrypted at rest. Filename coc-YYYY-MM-DD.log. At the bottom of the day's file, one signature line: the SHA-256 of the whole day's log. This is the file you will hand to counsel, unmodified, if the day's work is ever challenged.

Step 9 — Verify the hash chain weekly. Once a week, run a small verification pass: re-derive each day's ending signature from its contents, and confirm each day's opening line references the previous day's signature. If the chain breaks, you want to know within seven days, not eighteen months. The weekly pass takes under a minute and it is the reason the eighteen-month challenge does not surprise you.
section.subtitle: A worked case, dead ends and all
section.p: The matter reopens on a Wednesday morning in August 2026. The report you filed on 12 March 2025 argued, at moderate rung, that the subject had contradicted his own earlier public statement about a supply-chain contract signed with a mid-sized wholesaler in the northern Netherlands. The contradiction sat in a single tweet dated 4 March 2025, posted from an account that has since been deleted. The tweet said, roughly, that the subject "was never in the room" for the January meeting where the contract was outlined. Your report cited it as screenshot at page 9 (retrieved 12 March 2025, 13:07 UTC).

Opposing counsel writes, on behalf of the subject, that the tweet never existed. They imply — carefully, in the way counsel implies things — that the screenshot was constructed. They ask for the provenance of the artefact, in full.

You open the case folder. The report is in one subfolder. The chain-of-custody log is in a second subfolder that has not been touched in eighteen months and that verifies clean against the weekly signature you last ran two weeks before you filed. The log format itself is a shop choice — some practices keep the human-readable key=value line shown below, some keep the JSONL entry shown in Appendix B, both work — the discipline is pick one and stay with it across every case in the shop, so a reader who opens any log knows the shape without asking. The relevant line reads, in the log:
section.subtitle: coc entry 2025-03-12

p.code: form=canonical; also fetched share form (short URL) at 13:07:41Z

p.emphasis: The entry is thirteen lines. Nine of them are the anchors.

section.p: Now you walk it out. You re-fetch the archived HTML from the Wayback URL. You hash the bytes. You paste the hash into a terminal window and diff it against the SHA-256 in the log.
section.subtitle: verification console

p.emphasis: The hash matches the log line. The archive holds what you fetched.

section.p: That is the load-bearing move. If the hash had failed, the rest of the chain would be corroborative at best. Because it verifies, the archived HTML is what you fetched on 12 March 2025 at 13:07:22 UTC — the entire chain now rests on Wayback's timestamp, which is what you needed it to.

Dead end one. The archive.today snapshot, archive.ph/mQ8Vk, opens in a browser but the tweet's pinned first reply — where the subject had, ninety minutes earlier, quote-tweeted himself in a small edit that mattered to your reasoning — has been captured with the reply thread collapsed. archive.today rendered the top-level post but lost the expansion. The snapshot corroborates the tweet's existence and its timestamp; it does not corroborate the pinned reply your report never claimed to rely on anyway. You note the loss in your reply to counsel, and you move on.

Dead end two. You look, out of caution, at the Wayback capture and see something you do not like: the first Wayback fetch you triggered on 12 March at 13:07:44 UTC came back as a JavaScript shell — the loading spinner, the page skeleton, none of the content. You almost — and this is the eighteen-months-ago you, on the day — closed the log line and moved on with the archive.today capture only. You did not. You re-triggered Wayback a second time at 13:12:18 UTC, and that second capture is the one whose URL is in the log. The one that verifies. You know this because the log line references the 13:07:44 URL as alternate= in the next line down, marked unusable — JS shell. You wrote the failure down. It saved you.

Dead end three. Opposing counsel spots, and raises, a fifteen-minute delta between the archive.today capture (at 13:07:41Z, within seconds of your fetch) and the working Wayback capture (at 13:12:18Z). They imply the delta is suspicious. You show them the alternate log line: the first Wayback attempt was at 13:07:44Z, four seconds after the archive.today capture; it rendered as a JS shell; the retry succeeded four minutes later. The delta is not a gap in the chain, it is a documented failure of the first archive attempt. Counsel accepts it. The concept of a documented failure is what wins the exchange — an undocumented delta is a hole, a documented one is discipline.

Dead end four. Somewhere in the case-notes file — not the log, the notes — there is a screenshot of the same tweet with no capture-time overlay. You had taken it as a working image while you were writing the section for the report, and you had never written its capture time anywhere. If your entire chain had rested on that image, you would have been in trouble; the report would still stand as reasoning, but the artefact under it would be a rumour. The report did not rest on it. It rested on the log. The screenshot was a working aid, and working aids that are not in the log do not exist in a chain of custody. The lesson costs you a small embarrassed note back to your case-notes template.

What survives. The tweet's existence at 13:07:22 UTC on 4 March 2025 (via the Wayback capture, hash-verified against the log). The tweet's content, verbatim (same). The tweet's timestamp within the archived HTML (same). The subject's authorship as the account operator at that time (via the archive.today capture confirming the account handle and profile fields at 13:07:41Z). The report's citation of the artefact on 12 March 2025 as moderate — appropriate then, appropriate now — because a self-deleted tweet is a self-signalled record, not a first-party confirmation of the underlying claim.

What does not survive. The pinned reply, lost to archive.today's capture. Any inference from the pinned reply. The screenshot in the notes folder, which is now marked working aid, not evidence. You send counsel a two-page provenance letter with the log lines, the two archive URLs, the hash-verification console output, and the alternate-attempt line. Counsel replies the next morning that the matter is closed on that point. The report stands.
The eighteen-month challenge does not, in the end, feel dramatic. It feels routine, because you had already done the work in March 2025 to make it routine in August 2026.
section.subtitle: A second case: the one that doesn't close
section.p: The engagement lands cold in June 2026. The prior investigator left the firm; the case is thirteen months old; the client wants a supplementary opinion. The prior investigator's report cites eleven URLs across seven platforms and pages, none of them archived, no hashes, no capture times, no intent lines. Two of the eleven URLs are already dead; a third redirects to a domain-parking page. You spend two days trying to reconstruct chain-of-custody backwards from the report's prose.

You find Wayback captures adjacent to three of the eleven URLs, close enough in time that the content probably matches what the prior investigator saw; you can hash those and stand them up as reasonable proxy, not chain of custody. Four of the URLs return nothing on any archive. Two you re-derive by hunting for the content on quoter sites and rebuilding the reasoning downstream from a fresh chain that you do keep from scratch. Two you cannot reconstruct at all, and you write to the client that the two claims from the prior report that rested on those URLs cannot be supported without contact you are not willing to make.

The lesson is one line and it is the whole reason for this chapter. Provenance cannot be back-filled. You either kept the log or you did not. When the person before you did not, the honest work is to say so, in writing, to the client — and to refuse to warm-over the parts of the prior report that no longer stand up on evidence you can defend yourself.
section.subtitle: Chain-of-custody vs case notes
section.p: Two logs, always separate. The chain-of-custody log is evidence about evidence: URLs, timestamps, hashes, archive IDs, intent lines, signatures. It is boring on purpose. The case notes are your reasoning: hypotheses, pivots you tried, the moment you noticed a signal was collapsible, the paragraph where you decided a rung. The notes are where the thinking lives; the log is where the receipts live.

Do not merge them. When you merge them, two things happen. You corrupt the log — the reasoning-in-progress leaks into what should be flat, timestamped, and unopinionated. And you corrupt the notes — every stray thought now carries a hash next to it, and you begin to hesitate before writing down a wrong idea in progress, because the log is watching. Wrong ideas in progress are how correct findings are reached. Keep the notebook where you can be wrong out loud. Keep the log where you cannot.
The one bridge between them is a pointer. In the notes, when you cite an artefact, you cite the log line that anchors it — coc-2025-03-12 line 7 — not the URL itself. That is the only crossing.
section.subtitle: A safe exercise
section.p: Keep a provenance log for one week on nothing that matters. Your own routine web browsing — three URLs a day, chosen at random from what you already had open. For each, fix the URL forms, hash the fetched file, push it to Wayback and archive.today, record the capture UTC, write a one-sentence intent (checking the changelog for my own text editor, reading a recipe I want to keep, whatever it actually is), sign the line, and close it into the day's log. At the end of the week, verify the whole log. Notice how long it takes. Notice which steps you skipped without meaning to. Notice how it feels to open the log on day seven and see the whole week reconstructed cleanly. That reflex, learned on nothing, is the reflex you will reach for on the day the e-mail from opposing counsel arrives.
section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • An artefact without provenance is a rumour; five anchors turn it into evidence.
• URL, UTC, SHA-256, two independent preservation copies, one-line intent. In that order, every time.
• Preserve before you know whether the artefact will matter — chain of custody cannot be back-filled.
• Two archives is the floor; three is what you do when the matter is going to court.
• Sign each log line with a small hash that chains to the previous line; verify the chain weekly, not annually.
• Keep the chain-of-custody log separate from the case notes. Evidence about evidence in one place; your reasoning in another. Cross them only by pointer.
• A documented failure inside the log is discipline; an undocumented gap is a hole.
• The eighteen-month challenge is not dramatic if you did the work in the first week.
section.subtitle: What comes next
section.p: Chapter 4 turns from the log under the report to the report itself — the decision-grade document your client's counsel reads in five minutes and acts on.

p.emphasis: The document counsel reads in five minutes and acts on.

section.subtitle: Chapter Four
section.p: Counsel prints the report Friday morning at 07:45. She has a coffee, a candidate named Marcus Kettering, and a call at 09:00 with the CEO where she has to say whether the offer letter goes out or gets pulled. She reads the first page standing at the printer. She reads the second page walking back to her office. She sits down, opens a highlighter, and goes to the page that says what was ruled out.

She does not read the whole report. She never does. She reads the summary, the confidence line under each finding, the ruled-out section, and the limitations. If a finding is marked strong and the ruled-out section names the counter-explanation you tested, she circles it. If a finding is marked moderate and the limitations section says why, she circles that too. If any word in your prose goes further than the evidence in your notes, she stops reading, calls you, and asks what you actually meant. That call, on a Friday at 08:10, is the worst call in this profession.
Everything in this chapter is about not getting that call. Not because the finding was wrong — findings are sometimes wrong — but because the sentence was more confident than the finding.
section.subtitle: The idea
section.p: The report is the product. Every finding you develop must survive being written down for a reader who is not you and who will act on it in five minutes.
[[DIAGRAM: report-anatomy]]

p.emphasis: Five sections stacked in reading order — summary, findings with ladder, ruled-out, limitations, provenance — with counsel's eye tracking the outer two before it ever reaches the middle.

cite.p: The finding lives in your head. The report is the only version the client owns.

section.p: The report anatomy that survives contact with counsel has five anchor elements. Learn them as a shape.
• The summary — under two hundred words, decision-actionable, one confidence line per finding.
• The findings ladder — every finding named on the weak / moderate / strong / confirmed scale, in prose, with the signals underneath.
• The provenance table — every claim tied to a source URL, a capture timestamp, a snapshot ID, and a hash of any downloaded artefact.
• The limitations section — what you did not do, what you could not confirm, what a competent reader might assume and be wrong about.
• What was ruled out — the counter-explanations you actively tested and killed, and the ones that survived and constrain the finding.
section.subtitle: What counsel reads first
section.p: The summary and the ruled-out section. In that order, and often nothing else on the first pass.

An executive summary is not an abstract. It is not a paragraph of context. It is the finding in one sentence, the confidence rung in the second, and the recommendation in the third — repeated for every discrete finding the report carries. Two hundred words is a generous ceiling, not a target. If counsel cannot make the decision from the summary, the summary is broken; the rest of the report supports the summary, it does not replace it.

Under each finding, one confidence line. Not a paragraph. A sentence that names the rung and the number of independent signals underneath. Moderate, on two independent signals; one hard identifier would move it to strong. That is the sentence counsel reads. It tells her what she can quote to the CEO, what she cannot, and what would change if you had another day.

The decision-actionable recommendation is a separate sentence and does not appear in every report. Sometimes the recommendation is the record does not support proceeding without further check. Sometimes it is the record does not surface anything material to the engagement question. Sometimes it is nothing — you present the findings and counsel decides. Know which of those three is on the page before you send it.

The five-minute reading arc: summary, per-finding confidence line, ruled-out, limitations. If a reader who does that arc still has to call you to know what to do, you wrote a research memo, not a report.
section.subtitle: The five sections a decision-grade report must have
section.p: One — engagement scope recap. Two sentences. What the client asked, what you were retained to answer, what you were explicitly not retained to answer. Not the retainer boilerplate — the shape of the question, in the words the client used, so a reader in eighteen months can tell whether you answered it. If the client asked about a candidate's professional history and you found something about their private life, this section is where you name the boundary you did not cross.

Two — summary of findings with confidence tier per finding. The block counsel reads first. One sentence per finding, one confidence line per finding, one recommendation for the whole. Under two hundred words. Written last, revised twice.

Three — findings in detail, with provenance references inline. Each finding gets its own subsection. The finding as a sentence. The signals underneath it, numbered and named. Why the signals are independent of each other. The provenance references — snapshot IDs and hashes — cited inline, not tucked into a footnote counsel will not read. If a finding is strong, the section shows the three signals and their independence. If it is moderate, the section names why and what would move it to strong.

Four — what was ruled out. This is the section junior investigators skip because it feels like admitting weakness. It is the opposite. It is the section that proves you falsified. It names the counter-explanations you tested — namesake collision, timezone artefact, second person on a shared account, a photograph that looks like a match but resolves to a different date. For each, one line on how you ruled it out, or one line on why it remains an open residual and how it constrains the finding above. A report without a ruled-out section reads to counsel like a marketing document.

Five — limitations and open questions. What was outside scope. What you could not access. What a competent counter-investigator on the other side would have done to close the door you were walking through. What a follow-up engagement could still surface. Counsel needs this to know how much weight to give the report, and to know what to ask you next.
section.subtitle: The method, step by step
section.p: Step 1 — Draft the summary first, top-down. Before you write a single finding in detail, draft the summary as if you were writing it for a colleague who will read only that. If you cannot draft it, you do not have findings — you have material. Go back to your notes.

Step 2 — Rank every finding on the ladder before you write it up. Do the ranking as a separate pass, in your notes, not in the prose. The ladder is decided by the evidence in the case file, not by the sentence you were about to write. If a finding you were going to call strong is really moderate on two signals, it does not become strong because it fits better in the summary that way.

Step 3 — Write "what was ruled out" second, before the findings. This is the move that feels wrong and is right. Forcing yourself to name the counter-explanations before you write the findings is the last chance you have to falsify your own work. A finding that survives the ruled-out pass is a finding you can defend. A finding that does not survive gets rewritten or killed.

Step 4 — Quote provenance inline. Not in a footnote, not in a separate appendix nobody opens. Inside the sentence: snapshot ID arch-2026-08-11-1943Z-9a2f, captured 2026-08-11T19:43:07Z, artefact SHA-256 4e2c…. The reader can skip past the reference; a reviewer cannot. Both need it on the page.

Step 5 — Hedge language on strong, not only on weak. Weak findings hedge themselves — the word tells the reader what to do with them. Strong findings are where sentences get out ahead of the evidence, because the writer trusts the finding and stops policing the prose. That is where counsel gets burned. Write the strong sentence at the level a strong finding actually supports — not confirmed, because confirmed is a self-link, and this is not one.

Step 6 — Let a peer read it. The peer's job is not to agree. The peer's job is to find the sentence that goes further than the evidence, the finding that is one source dressed as two, and the ruled-out section that is thin. Chapter 8 is where the team-facing side of this lives — for now, know that a report a peer has not read is a draft, not a report.

Step 7 — Cut fifteen percent. After the peer read, before you send it, cut fifteen percent. The paragraphs you love are usually the ones counsel will not read. The sentences you added to sound thorough are the ones the subject's lawyer will quote back at you. Short is not a style choice. It is a survival trait.

Try it (2026). Take one case finding from Volume 3 — the operator-cluster attribution from Chapter 6, or the Purnell reconstruction from Chapter 1. Rewrite it as a two-paragraph counsel-ready micro-report: one paragraph of summary with a confidence line, one paragraph of one finding in detail with provenance references and one ruled-out counter-explanation. Read it aloud. If any word carries further than the evidence in the original chapter, cut it. Then cut fifteen percent more.
section.subtitle: Language a lawyer will accept
section.p: The sentence is where competent work most often gets rewritten by an editor or served with a letter. The finding was defensible; the sentence was not. Pair each rejected form with the accepted form, understand why the rejected form fails, and keep the pairing near your keyboard. These are the eight patterns that break reports.
• Rejected: Marcus Kettering appears to be the same person as the account m.kettering.dev on GitHub.
• Accepted: The account m.kettering.dev self-links to kettering-marcus.com in its GitHub bio; the same domain is named in Marcus Kettering's résumé as his portfolio site.

• Why the rejected form fails: appears to be is a hedge that hides a real inference. It reads like humility and functions like a claim you did not source. State the self-link and let the reader do the identification.
• Rejected: He worked at Halberd Systems from 2019 to 2022.

• Accepted: A LinkedIn profile at linkedin.com/in/mkettering-914 (captured 2026-08-11T09:14:02Z, snapshot arch-…-914) lists employment at Halberd Systems, 2019–2022. The dates match a payroll reference confirmed by the client on 2026-08-12.
• Why the rejected form fails: it is a fact without a source. In a report, an unsourced sentence reads as your personal knowledge, and personal knowledge is what depositions are built on.
• Rejected: We cannot rule out that Kettering held a second role during this period.
• Accepted: The record does not support a second role during this period. A second role remains possible; the sources checked did not surface one.

• Why the rejected form fails: cannot rule out is a double negative that a lay reader flips into a positive. Counsel who quotes cannot rule out to the CEO has, in the CEO's ear, just said there was a second role. Write the negation as an absence, not a failure.
• Rejected: This is his account.

• Accepted: The account is attributed to Marcus Kettering at strong, on three independent signals: (i) the self-link from github.com/m-kettering to kettering-marcus.com, (ii) the reuse of the profile photograph across LinkedIn and a 2022 conference speaker page, and (iii) the identical spelling of his middle initial J. across three unrelated records.

• Why the rejected form fails: this is his is a claim without a rung. The reader has no way to know how sure you are, and neither does the record. Name the rung and the signals, or do not make the claim.
• Rejected: Kettering has poor operational security.

• Accepted: Kettering's public accounts across three platforms reuse the same handle and the same profile photograph. The pattern is consistent with a subject who has not attempted to compartmentalise his public presence.
• Why the rejected form fails: poor is a value word. It reads as your judgement of the subject rather than as an observation of the record. Report what is on the record; let counsel judge.
• Rejected: Kettering recently updated his LinkedIn profile to remove the Halberd role.

• Accepted: A snapshot of linkedin.com/in/mkettering-914 captured on 2026-08-04T11:22:19Z lists the Halberd role. A snapshot captured on 2026-08-14T13:07:22Z does not. The change occurred within that window.

• Why the rejected form fails: recently is a word with no referent. It means different things to a reader in September than to a reader in January. Every temporal claim in a report needs a bracket, and the bracket needs a UTC timestamp.
• Rejected: Jane Doe wrote the 2021 blog post criticising Halberd.

• Accepted: A user posting as jane_doe_1988 on the blog hardware-notes.example.net wrote the 2021 post criticising Halberd. The identity behind the handle has not been established from the record checked.

• Why the rejected form fails: naming a subject by a real-world identity when the record only supports a handle is the specific mistake that gets findings thrown out and reports served with retraction demands. A handle is not a person until a hard identifier says it is.
• Rejected: We know that Kettering left Halberd under difficult circumstances.

• Accepted: The record shows a nine-month employment gap on his LinkedIn profile between 2022 and 2023. The record does not carry a reason for the gap; the client may wish to ask the candidate directly.

• Why the rejected form fails: we know claims knowledge the record does not carry, and it invites the reader to treat the sentence as fact. The record shows keeps the sentence tied to what is actually in the case file. The distinction between what you know and what the record shows is the single most useful discipline in this profession.
The rule under all of them: write the sentence you would be willing to read back, aloud, in a deposition. If any word in it goes further than the evidence in the case file, cut that word.
section.subtitle: A worked case, dead ends and all
section.p: An HR director at a Portland engineering firm — call her Ana Vollmer — retains you on a Monday to vet a senior candidate for a director-of-platform role. The candidate: Marcus J. Kettering, thirty-eight, résumé listing Halberd Systems 2019–2022, an independent consultancy 2022–2024, and a current role at a firm called Prospect Rail. Scope: professional history, public conduct, undisclosed conflicts. Out of scope: private life, family, medical. Deliverable: a decision-grade report by Thursday evening for Friday morning counsel review.
You spend Tuesday and Wednesday in the record. By Thursday morning you have six candidate findings in your notes.
• F1: Kettering's professional handle across GitHub, LinkedIn, and a 2022 conference speaker page is m-kettering / mkettering-914 / m.kettering.dev, self-linked and photograph-matched. Strong.
• F2: A LinkedIn edit between 2026-08-04 and 2026-08-14 removed the Halberd role from the profile. Strong, on two dated snapshots.

• F3: A blog handle jane_doe_1988 on a small hardware blog wrote a 2021 post criticising Halberd's engineering culture, later cited in a Hacker News thread that Kettering commented on. You had convinced yourself, on Wednesday afternoon, that jane_doe_1988 was Kettering under a pseudonym. Strong, you wrote in the margin.

• F4: A photograph on the 2022 conference speaker page places Kettering at a venue in Porto in October 2022 — a period his consultancy engagement records list as full-time on a client project in Berlin. Moderate.
• F5: A GitHub commit history under m.kettering.dev shows continuous activity through the LinkedIn nine-month gap. Moderate.
• F6: A domain prospect-rail-internal.example.io registered in 2024 shares a JARM fingerprint with two other domains registered by a Prospect Rail engineer named separately in the record. Weak.
You draft the summary Wednesday evening, feeling clean. You draft the findings-in-detail on Thursday morning. On Thursday at 11:00 your peer reads the draft.
The peer kills three findings.

F3 — the jane_doe_1988 attribution — was one source dressed as two. You had the blog handle, and you had a Hacker News comment from Kettering that engaged with the blog post at length. You had convinced yourself the engagement was self-quotation. The peer pointed out, in one sentence, that engaging with a blog post is not the same as writing it, and that the only signal tying the handle to Kettering was your own inference. F3 moves out of findings and into what was ruled out, with a line naming the residual: the handle remains unattributed; the tone of Kettering's comment does not attribute it.

F4 — the Porto photograph — you had ranked moderate. The peer pointed at the photograph itself: it was on a speaker page dated October 2022, but the photograph in it was undated, and the venue was one Kettering had also spoken at in 2019. The photograph was probably re-used. F4 downgrades from moderate to weak, and moves into limitations rather than findings, because a weak signal about a private-life inference is not something to put in a decision-grade report at all.

F6 — the JARM fingerprint — was outside scope. Prospect Rail is Kettering's current employer, not the subject. Investigating another Prospect Rail engineer through infrastructure pivots was you following the pivot instead of the scope. F6 comes out entirely, and gets a note in the ruled-out section: infrastructure signals adjacent to the subject's current employer were noted and not developed; they are outside scope.

You had written the summary Wednesday night around six findings. On Thursday at 12:30 you throw the summary out and rewrite it around three: F1 (strong), F2 (strong), and F5, which after the peer read has been re-examined and ranked moderate on two independent signals — the commit history under m.kettering.dev and a distinct commit-timestamp cluster falling inside Pacific business hours across three of the nine gap months, consistent with the timezone Kettering's résumé claims for that period. The overlap of activity with the LinkedIn gap is the framing of the finding, not a second signal; the peer catches that in the margin before you write the paragraph. Two of the paragraphs you loved most in the Wednesday draft are gone. That is the job.

A provenance note you cannot retrieve at write-time: a Wayback snapshot you had cited for F2 will not resolve on Thursday afternoon. You have the artefact hash and the capture time in your log, but the archive is timing out. You leave the citation in with a note that the snapshot ID is recorded in the case file at a specific path, and that the archive was unreachable at report time. Better to name the gap than to hide it.

The final report goes to Vollmer at 16:45 Thursday. On Friday morning at 07:45, counsel prints it. She reads the summary and the ruled-out section. Two findings are strong and named to sources. One is moderate with a clear line on what would move it. Nothing about the candidate's private life is in the report; nothing about Prospect Rail's infrastructure is either. Counsel calls the CEO at 09:00 and recommends proceeding with a targeted question to the candidate about the nine-month gap. The offer letter goes out the following week, with a paragraph the candidate signs acknowledging the gap.
Here is what one paragraph of the report looked like, in the finished draft:

section.subtitle: A second case: the one that doesn't close
section.p: A different engagement, the following month. Vollmer sends over a second candidate, a senior compliance hire named Rita Kowalska. You do the work Monday through Wednesday. Every finding tops out at moderate. Her professional handle is consistent across three platforms, but you have no self-link that would elevate the identity attribution to strong. The gap in her employment history has a plausible reading (parental leave, referenced obliquely in a 2021 conference bio) and does not resolve to a hard identifier either way. Nothing on the public record contradicts the résumé; nothing corroborates it beyond what a hiring manager could see themselves.

The report goes to Vollmer with three moderate findings and a limitations section that names what a strong answer would have required. Counsel reads it Friday morning, thanks you, and does not act. The offer letter goes out unchanged. Vollmer pays the invoice and books you again in October.

That is a real outcome, not a failure. The report is the deliverable. The decision belongs to counsel. A report that honestly says moderate is worth more than a report that dresses moderate as strong to feel useful.
section.subtitle: What NOT to put in a report
section.p: Speculation. Opinion. Editorial commentary about the subject's character, choices, or private life. Extra background you researched that did not become a finding — no matter how interesting, no matter how much you liked it. Screenshots without a provenance reference underneath them. Anything about a person adjacent to the subject who was not in scope, even if you found something. Anything about the client's competitor or industry that you learned along the way. The tool names and query strings you used — the client did not retain you for a method paper. Any sentence beginning we believe or we suspect or it seems. Any joke. Any adjective doing rhetorical work rather than descriptive work.
A report is what the client bought. Everything else is your own notes. Keep the notes; do not ship them.
section.subtitle: A safe exercise
section.p: Take one case from Volume 3 — the Purnell reconstruction from Chapter 1, or the operator-cluster attribution from Chapter 6, or the geolocation from Chapter 4. Write the two-paragraph counsel-summary version: one summary paragraph with a decision-actionable recommendation, one paragraph carrying the strongest finding with its confidence rung and its three signals. Under two hundred words. Then read it aloud, cut every word that goes further than the evidence, and cut fifteen percent more. What survives is the shape of a decision-grade report.
section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • The report is the product; every finding must survive being written down for a reader who is not you.
• Counsel reads the summary and the ruled-out section first — the five-minute arc decides whether the report gets used.
• Five sections, in order: scope recap, summary with confidence lines, findings in detail with inline provenance, what was ruled out, limitations and open questions.
• Draft the summary first, top-down, and write what was ruled out before you write the findings — that is where falsification happens.
• Hedge language on strong findings, not only on weak ones — that is where sentences get ahead of evidence.
• Every temporal claim carries a UTC bracket; every attribution names its rung and its independent signals; every negation reads as absence, not as failure.
• What the record shows is not what you know — keep the sentence tied to the case file.
• Cut fifteen percent after the peer read. The paragraphs you love are usually the ones counsel will not read.
section.subtitle: What comes next
section.p: The next chapter turns to the specific engagement most working investigators earn their living on — pre-hire vetting and due-diligence work — and the legal frames that decide what you can look at, and what you can put in the report if you do.

title.p: What the Frame Lets You See

p.emphasis: Vetting is the discipline of looking hard at what you are allowed to look at, and reporting only what you are allowed to report.

section.subtitle: Chapter Five
section.p: Nadia Karel calls at 08:12 on a Monday. She is the head of people at Kessel Logistiek, a mid-sized logistics operator out of Rotterdam, and she has a candidate she wants to sign by Friday. The candidate is a senior hire — VP of Operations, reporting to the COO — and the process has been running for six weeks. Two rounds with the executive team, a case interview, references that came back clean. What she does not have is the last piece: a pre-hire vetting report she can put in front of her general counsel before the offer letter goes out. She has done this five times with you. She knows what she gets, she knows what she does not. Her opening line is the one she always uses. Same scope, same deliverable, Friday morning.

You take the notes as she speaks. Elin Foss, forty-one, current title at Aker Biosolutions in Oslo, prior roles across two logistics firms in the Netherlands and one in Sweden. Résumé on file. Written consent from the candidate on file — Nadia's HR team collected it during the offer stage, standard clause, standard scope. The candidate knows a vetting will be done. That is not the same as the candidate having pre-authorised any specific search, and Nadia knows that too. The scope is professional history, public conduct, undisclosed conflicts. Private life, family, health, protected characteristics — out of scope, and, as you will see this week, not merely out of scope but out of the report even where the record surfaces them.
You open a fresh case folder at 08:34. You do not open a browser tab until 09:15. What happens in the intervening forty minutes is this chapter.
section.subtitle: The idea
section.p: Vetting is not a search; it is a search inside a frame, and the frame is decided before you start.
[[DIAGRAM: vetting-frames]]

p.emphasis: Two concentric rings. The outer ring is what the client wants to know; the inner ring is what the frame — statute, contract, and jurisdiction — allows you to look at and report. The craft is the gap between them, held honestly on both sides.

cite.p: The frame is not a limitation on the work. The frame is the work.

section.p: The anchor elements of a vetting engagement — the ones that survive across pre-hire, executive-protection, insider-risk, and board vetting alike — are these:
• The scope, written down before you look, in the client's words and yours, naming both what you are retained to answer and what you are explicitly not.

• The frame, named by jurisdiction and instrument — the statute, the contract clause, the notice that was served — so that at report time you can point at the sentence that says why a section is silent.
• The consent record, kept as an artefact, not as a memory of a phone call.
• The type of engagement, distinguished on paper, because the tolerance for a moderate finding on an executive-protection matter is not the tolerance for a moderate finding on a junior hire.
• The report boundary, decided before the first search, so that a finding you cannot report does not accidentally leak through the sentence you liked.
section.subtitle: The legal frames, briefly
section.p: The frame is a sidebar to the craft, not the fabric of it. What you need in your head as a working investigator is enough to know when you are in a frame, which one, and when the answer to a scope question is ask counsel rather than look it up. The paragraphs below are the working shape of the four frames you will meet most; every case will still turn on counsel's read of the specific engagement.

FCRA, in the United States. A pre-employment background check produced by a third party is a consumer report under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, whether you called it that or not. The permissible-purpose recital your engagement letter carries is §1681b(a)(3)(B) — employment. If you are the third party producing it, you are — for that engagement — a Consumer Reporting Agency, and the candidate has a right to notice, to consent, and, if any information in your report contributes to a decision not to hire, to a two-step adverse-action process the employer runs under §1681b(b)(3): a pre-adverse-action notice with a copy of the report and a summary of rights, a reasonable waiting period (five business days is the field-standard floor, not a statute), then a final adverse-action notice. A subtlety worth knowing early: a report that reaches into interviews of former colleagues or neighbours becomes an investigative consumer report under §1681d, with its own additional disclosures. And §613 sets a distinct discipline for public-record items that could adversely affect the candidate — you either notify the candidate contemporaneously, or you maintain strict procedures to ensure the record is current. If you do not know whether FCRA applies to your engagement, you assume it does until counsel says otherwise. It is cheaper to be careful than to be sued. Do not draft an adverse-action letter yourself; that is counsel's paragraph, not yours.

EEOC and protected classes, alongside FCRA. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission does not care what you researched; it cares what a hiring decision was made on. Protected classes — race, colour, religion, sex, national origin, age, disability, genetic information, pregnancy — are the categories a report must not surface, must not weigh, and, in most cases, must not mention even to acknowledge that you avoided them. If you saw a religious affiliation in a public Reddit post, the report is silent on it. If you saw a pregnancy hint on a subreddit, the report is silent on it. The silence is deliberate, and the note that explains the silence goes to counsel, not into the report.

GDPR and national DPAs, in the European Union. Vetting personal data is processing under the General Data Protection Regulation. The lawful basis for that processing is not obvious and it is decided by the client's counsel, not by you: sometimes legitimate interest under Article 6(1)(f) with a documented balancing test, sometimes contractual necessity, rarely consent — because consent under GDPR must be freely given, and the power imbalance between candidate and employer means several DPAs (notably the AEPD in Spain and the Garante in Italy) do not accept consent as a lawful basis for pre-hire vetting at all.

A systematic vetting engagement will typically also require a Data Protection Impact Assessment under Article 35, and a legitimate-interest balancing test that a competent DPA will read the way counsel reads a report. You do not draft the DPIA or the balancing test; the client's counsel or DPO does. What you do is confirm the DPIA and balancing test are on file before you open a tab, and refuse the engagement if they are not.

Try it (2026). Take a fictional senior-hire engagement in your own jurisdiction. Write the frame paragraph you would put at the top of the case file — three sentences: (a) which statute the frame invokes; (b) which lawful basis your client's counsel is expected to name; (c) which sentence you would refuse the engagement on. Compare against the paragraph at the top of your last live engagement. If they differ, the difference is worth a conversation with counsel before your next intake.

The UK, and everything else. In the United Kingdom, the Data Protection Act 2018 and the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations do a lot of the same work as GDPR with local nuances; the ICO's guidance on investigative processing is where counsel will start. In every other jurisdiction — Canada's PIPEDA, Brazil's LGPD, Singapore's PDPA, and the growing patchwork of US state privacy laws (California CPRA, Virginia VCDPA, Colorado CPA) — the shape is the same: name the frame, get counsel to confirm the lawful basis, and stay inside what the basis permits. You do not need to memorise the statutes; you need to know which one your engagement lives under, and you need counsel who will decide whether a specific check is proportionate.

The line at the top of every vetting engagement, in bold, at the head of the case file, is the one you should be able to recite without opening the folder: counsel decides what the frame permits; you check what you are allowed to look at, and you report only what you are allowed to report. Everything in this chapter sits below that line.
section.subtitle: Before you look
section.p: Get the consent record on your desk in a form you can point at. A signed clause in an offer letter, a countersigned engagement notice, a data-processing addendum with the client — one of these, dated, and cited in the case file by document ID. The vetting starts when the record is on the desk. Not before.

Read the engagement letter for the sentence that names the deliverable and the recipient. The report goes to counsel or to the client's HR function under counsel's oversight — not to the hiring manager directly, not to the CEO's inbox, not to the candidate. If your engagement letter does not name the recipient, ask before you look.

Confirm scope in writing with the client on the same day the engagement opens. Two lines back to Nadia at 09:00: scope is professional history, public conduct, undisclosed conflicts; out of scope is private life, family, health, protected characteristics; deliverable is a decision-grade report to counsel by Friday 12:00 CET. Save her reply into the case folder. That is the artefact you cite in the scope-recap section of the report.
Then, and only then, open a browser tab.
section.subtitle: The method, step by step
section.p: Step 1 — Fix the identity before you look at the record. Full legal name, date of birth if the consent record gives it to you, jurisdictions of prior residence and employment. Namesake collisions are the single most common way vetting engagements go wrong; a wrong-person hit that you carry into the report will be quoted back at you in the deposition. The first hour is spent narrowing the identity, not searching the record. Every subsequent finding is anchored to the identity you fixed here.

Step 2 — Name the frame in the case file. One paragraph at the top of your notes, in your own words: which jurisdiction the engagement sits under, which statute the frame invokes, what the consent record permits, what the scope excludes. This is the paragraph you re-read every time you are tempted to open a tab that is out of scope. Its function is to save you from yourself at 15:00 on a Wednesday when a curiosity thread beckons.

Step 3 — Walk the professional record first. Résumé claims, in order. Each employer named, each role, each date range. For each, the first-party sources — company registries where they exist (Companies House, the KVK, the Bolagsverket, the SEC), the archived versions of the employer's own site, the LinkedIn record captured with a UTC timestamp and a snapshot ID as Chapter 3 requires. Walking the résumé claim by claim is dull work. It is also the work that produces the strongest findings.

Step 4 — Public conduct, framed by the engagement type. Public writing, conference speaking, quoted statements in press. For a pre-hire junior role, this is a light pass. For a senior hire, it is deeper. For executive protection, it is deeper still, because the personal-safety context changes the calculus of what a subject's public exposure implies. For an insider-risk engagement, it is different again — you are looking for pattern change against a baseline you have from the client. Know which of the four you are on, and calibrate the pass accordingly.

Try it (2026). Take a public figure whose professional record is well-covered — a mid-tier CEO of a mid-cap public company, someone whose SEC filings and LinkedIn history are already in the public record. Draft the scope of a vetting engagement for them in three lines: what you would look at, what you would not, and which frame you would name at the top of the case file if the engagement were run out of your own jurisdiction. Do not run any searches. The exercise is in the drafting.

Step 5 — Undisclosed conflicts, on paper. Directorships, ownership stakes, adjacent consultancies, side entities. The registries are your friend. A KVK filing, a Companies House officer record, a state-level LLC lookup — these are the sources that produce strong findings, because they are first-party filings the subject signed. Cross-check the entities named in the subject's LinkedIn interests and volunteer experience sections; the disclosure the subject wrote themselves is often the disclosure the client's onboarding form did not ask for.

Step 6 — Guard the boundary as you go. Every hour, look at the last three tabs you opened and ask whether they are inside the frame. A tab on a subject's spouse is out. A tab on a subject's minor child is out and closed. A tab on a subreddit that touches a protected class is out; the tab closes, and the observation does not enter the case file even as a marginal note. This is the discipline that makes the report writable.

Step 7 — Ladder every finding as you develop it, not at report time. Weak for a single unattributed signal. Moderate for two independent signals. Strong for three, or for two with a hard identifier under one. Confirmed only when the subject self-links from a first-party account to a first-party document — and never by stacking moderates. Chapter 3 is where the case file lives; the ladder is decided in the notes, in ink, before the sentence in the report goes anywhere near it.

Step 8 — Kill what the frame forbids you to report, and note the kill. If a finding is inside your case file but outside your report boundary, it comes out of the report and stays in the case file with a one-line note to counsel: observed but not reported; reason: protected class or reason: outside scope or reason: private life. Counsel does not want to read the observation; counsel wants to know you saw it, chose not to carry it, and named the reason. That note travels to counsel in a separate channel, not in the deliverable.

Step 9 — Adverse-action prep, if the frame requires it. In an FCRA engagement, if the report contains material that could contribute to an adverse decision, the client will need to serve the candidate with a pre-adverse-action packet. Your job is not to serve it; your job is to know that your report may trigger it, to flag findings that could sit at the heart of an adverse decision, and to be ready to produce a version of the report the candidate can be given. That readiness lives in the case file from Step 1, not in a scramble on Friday afternoon.
section.subtitle: A worked case, dead ends and all
section.p: Elin Foss, forty-one. Résumé on file: Aker Biosolutions 2023–present, Nordholm Logistiek 2019–2023, a stint at a Rotterdam operator called Van Beek Handel 2016–2019, and, before that, three years in Sweden at a firm the résumé lists as TrelleborgFrakt. Consent record signed 2026-07-28. Frame: engagement sits under Dutch law, GDPR, with a legitimate-interest basis documented by Kessel's own DPO in a memo Nadia forwarded to your case file at 09:47. Scope confirmed by return e-mail at 09:52.

Monday afternoon eats itself on a namesake. A Stockholm-based marketing consultant named Elin Foss, thirty-four, has an active LinkedIn, a personal blog, and a set of Instagram posts from a 2024 conference in Malmö. The photograph on the blog is a plausible partial match to the résumé photograph the candidate provided — same eye colour, similar hair, similar age bracket. You spend three hours ruling her out. It ends with a passport-verified date of birth on your candidate's consent record (1985-04-18) and a public speaker bio on the Stockholm Foss's blog naming her graduation year (2013) and undergraduate university (Umeå, not Uppsala, which the résumé names for the candidate). The two Elins are not the same person. That collision costs half a day and produces nothing you can put in a report. It also saves the report from a wrong-person finding, which is the trade you make with your time on every vetting engagement whether you feel it or not.

Tuesday morning, you walk the professional record. Aker Biosolutions is confirmed via the Brønnøysundregistrene officer record and an archived version of Aker's own leadership page at web.archive.org/web/2025*/aker-biosolutions.example.no/leadership captured on 2026-03-04T10:12:44Z. Nordholm Logistiek is confirmed via a KVK filing showing Elin Foss as a former officer (dates 2019–2023) and a payroll confirmation the client obtains directly and forwards to you at 14:20 on Tuesday. Van Beek Handel is trickier — the firm dissolved in 2020 and its website is gone — but the KVK record retains the officer roster for the period, and Elin Foss is named there for 2016–2019.

A Reddit thread from 2022, on a subreddit about logistics operations, is posted by a user elin_f_1985 whose profile you can see and whose posting history includes two comments that reference my daughter and one comment on a subreddit that touches a protected characteristic. You capture the thread ID and the timestamps into your case file, note that the account is not attributed by any self-link, and mark the private-life observations observed, not reported; reason: private life and protected class. Nothing from this line enters the report. It goes into your parallel note to counsel with two lines of context, so that counsel knows why the report is silent on a subreddit you clearly saw.

Wednesday morning, the timezone artefact. An Instagram post from 2023 shows a photograph you had convinced yourself was Elin Foss at a Van Beek Handel farewell event, on a date that would place her in Rotterdam ten days after the KVK filing shows her having moved to Nordholm Logistiek. The timestamp on the platform reads 2023-04-27T08:14:00 in your local view, which is Amsterdam time. When you re-fetch the post with the raw timestamp from the platform's API view, the created_at is 2023-04-26T22:14:00Z. The account posting the photograph is a former Van Beek colleague. The event was on the twenty-sixth, not the twenty-seventh, and the Nordholm start date on the KVK filing is the twenty-eighth. There is no discrepancy; the platform's local rendering had put her in Rotterdam a day later than the raw UTC does. A finding that would have been moderate on a résumé inconsistency dies in the notes and never reaches the report. The provenance of the kill goes into the case file so that if anyone asks in six months, you can walk them to the UTC line.

The finding that survives is on paper and it is signed. A Dutch KVK filing shows Elin Foss as the sole officer of an active advisory entity, Foss Advisory B.V., registered 2024-06-11. The filing lists the address at a Rotterdam co-working space and the website field at foss-advisory.example.nl. That domain, archived at web.archive.org/web/2025*/foss-advisory.example.nl/ on 2026-02-14T09:33:12Z, carries a client list. One of the three named clients is De Groot Transport, a direct competitor of Kessel Logistiek in the North Sea container corridor. The candidate's LinkedIn does not name the Foss Advisory entity. Her Aker employment contract, which the client obtained from her under the offer process and forwarded to you Wednesday, contains a standard non-compete but no active disclosure of the Foss Advisory entity or of the De Groot engagement. The chain is: KVK filing self-links to foss-advisory.example.nl in the website field; the archived site self-links back to the candidate by name in the About section; the site lists De Groot Transport as a current client on the same page. Strong, on three independent signals, one of which is a subject self-link.

A second finding, weaker: the candidate's LinkedIn description of her 2022 role at Nordholm lists interim CFO for a four-month period. The KVK officer filing does not list her as CFO at any point. The role may have been operational rather than a statutory appointment — a plausible reading — but the résumé sentence overstates what the filing supports. Moderate, on two independent signals from public first-party sources: the LinkedIn text and the KVK record. Would move to strong only with an internal Nordholm document that a competent counter-investigator could not obtain from the public record, and which counsel may or may not ask the candidate to produce.

The final report goes to Nadia at 11:40 on Friday. It carries two findings: the Foss Advisory conflict at strong, and the Nordholm role description at moderate. It carries no reference to the subreddit account. It carries no reference to the private-life signals. It carries a one-line limitations note that a data-only pass on Dutch registries does not fully corroborate the Nordholm role description, and that counsel may wish to invite the candidate to clarify. The parallel note to counsel names, without detail, the categories on which the report is silent and the reasons: private life, protected class, out of scope. Counsel reads both by 13:00. The offer letter does not go out Friday. It goes out the following Wednesday, after the candidate has been asked about the Foss Advisory entity and has, in her reply, disclosed the De Groot engagement and offered to terminate it as a condition of joining Kessel. That reply is the deliverable that closes the engagement. Yours was the paragraph that made the reply possible.
section.subtitle: A second case: the one that doesn't close
section.p: Two weeks later, Nadia sends you a mid-level ops candidate — Dieter Almqvist, thirty-three, one prior employer, a clean résumé, no obvious signals in the first hour. You do the work carefully through Tuesday and Wednesday. Every finding tops out at moderate. His professional handle is consistent across two platforms but has no self-link that would elevate identity attribution to strong. A short employment gap in 2021 has a plausible reading — a graduate programme he abandoned, referenced obliquely in a conference bio — and does not resolve to a hard identifier either way. Nothing on the public record contradicts the résumé; nothing corroborates it beyond what a competent hiring manager could see themselves.

The report goes to Nadia with three moderate findings and a limitations section naming what a strong answer would have required. Counsel reads it Friday, thanks you, and does not recommend adverse action. The offer letter goes out unchanged. Nadia pays the invoice and books you again for the next hire. That is a real outcome, not a failure. The decision belongs to counsel; the report is honest about the rung it can support.
section.subtitle: On what the frame forbids you to report
section.p: In the Foss engagement, you saw a Reddit post that carried a plausible pregnancy hint, a comment on a subreddit that named a religious affiliation, and a photograph on a personal blog that would let a reader guess at a health condition. None of the three is in the report. None of the three is even implied by omission — you did not write a sentence that would let a careful reader deduce that you had looked and chosen not to report. The section is silent, and the silence is total.

The parallel note to counsel names each category by its statutory label — protected class under EEOC-equivalent frame, sensitive category under GDPR Article 9 — and says, in one line each, that the report is silent on the category and why. Counsel does not need the observations; counsel needs to know that the silence in the report was a decision, not an oversight. That is the difference between a vetting report that survives scrutiny and one that does not. You saw what you saw; you reported what the frame permits; you told counsel where the frame drew the line. The subject's private life stays in the subject's private life.
section.subtitle: A safe exercise
section.p: Vet yourself. Write down your full legal name, date of birth, and jurisdictions of prior residence and employment. Draft a one-paragraph scope for a pre-hire engagement on yourself, in the frame of your own jurisdiction. Walk the professional record — your own registries, your own archived pages, your own LinkedIn history — as if you were a stranger with a signed consent notice on the desk. Rank the findings on the ladder. Then draft the parallel note to counsel: what you saw that the frame would forbid you from reporting, and why. The exercise takes an afternoon. It is the fastest way to understand, in your own skin, why the frame is the work.
section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • Vetting is a search inside a frame, not a search; the frame is named on paper before the first tab opens.
• Pre-hire, executive protection, insider risk, and board vetting are four different engagements with four different tolerances; know which one you are on.
• FCRA, EEOC-equivalent, GDPR, and national DPAs decide what the frame permits; counsel decides; you check.
• The consent record is an artefact you cite by document ID, not a memory of a phone call.
• Fix identity in the first hour; namesakes are the most common way a vetting engagement produces a wrong-person finding.
• Every finding is ladder-ranked in the notes before it reaches the report; confirmed is reserved for a subject self-link and is never reached by stacking moderates.
• Observations that fall outside the report boundary go to counsel in a parallel note that names the category and the reason; the report itself is silent, and the silence is deliberate.
• The report contains what the frame permits; the case file contains what you saw; the two are not the same document.
section.subtitle: What comes next
section.p: The next chapter turns the lens the other way, onto counter-OSINT — how a competent subject narrows the surface you have been walking through, and what that means for the vetting work you have just learned to do inside the frame.

p.emphasis: Counter-OSINT from both chairs — the defender who closed the door, and you standing in front of it.

section.subtitle: Chapter Six
section.p: The engagement lands on a Wednesday. A private-equity partner wants a soft-touch background on a founder his fund is considering leading a Series B into. Name, résumé, current company, three references. He needs you to pull the usual public-web work by Friday. Ninety-minute call, four thousand euro.

You open the folder Thursday morning. The founder's WHOIS is behind a privacy service, and the name-servers do not leak an internal domain. His LinkedIn is present but stripped — a title, a company name, no work history before 2023. There is no public GitHub under any variant of his name. There is no company blog written in his voice. The old-press-release search that worked in 2021 returns three trade-press mentions of the current company and nothing under his name older than eighteen months. His photograph on the fund's site is a professional headshot with the metadata cleaned. His Twitter has forty-three followers and one post: a link to the company page.
You sit back in the chair. Somewhere between the third dead pivot and the fourth, a voice in your head says the quiet part out loud: raise the fee estimate.
You are not looking at a founder who forgot to lock the door. You are looking at one who read the same three books you did.
section.subtitle: The idea
section.p: A competent subject who has done their own OSINT audit before you did yours has moved the shape of the work; you are no longer collecting a trail, you are triangulating around an absence.
[[DIAGRAM: counter-osint-map]]

p.emphasis: Two chairs on either side of the same table — the subject's audit map on one side, the investigator's pivot list on the other, the crossed-out lines matching, the surviving lines short and load-bearing.

cite.p: A door that is closed is still a door. It tells you where the house is.

section.p: The counter-OSINT posture — whether you are advising a client, cleaning up your own footprint, or running into it as an investigator — has a small number of anchor elements. Learn them as a shape.
• The self-audit as first defence. The subject who defends well starts by mapping their own footprint the way an attacker would, three months before they need to.
• Compartmentalisation, not deletion. One email per purpose, one number per identity, separate handles for separate audiences. Deletion is loud. Compartmentalisation is quiet.
• Domain and infrastructure hygiene. Privacy WHOIS is the first line, but it is not the interesting one — CAA records, cert scoping, and archive-conscious publication are.
• Photograph hygiene with realistic limits. Strip EXIF, obscure faces where it matters, understand that background triangulation still works and cannot be defeated by an EXIF stripper.
• Social-graph hygiene. A private profile still leaks through the comment threads, reactions, and friend-of-friend tags of every account that is not private.
• Text-fingerprint hygiene. Cadence, punctuation, and vocabulary survive a change of handle and are the residue nobody thinks about.
• The honest ceiling. Competent defence buys time and privacy, not invisibility.
section.subtitle: What died since 2023
section.p: The era when a real e-mail address sat in nine out of ten WHOIS records is over. Registrar-side privacy is now default in most consumer registrars, and the older records that carried the address have been overwritten in current lookups; they still exist in historical WHOIS databases, but the current record no longer hands you the address in the first hit.

The era when facesearch returned useful matches on any public photograph is also over — at least for the tools that were the field standard in 2020. The remaining public-facing services have narrower coverage and heavier friction. Some jurisdictions have started blocking indexing of biometric-matched hits at the platform level. This does not mean facesearch is dead; it means the tool is different and the confidence rungs it produces are lower.

The era when a LinkedIn work-history was assumed complete has passed on the professional side too. Enough people now curate their public LinkedIn presence for their next employer's counter-investigator that a clean profile is no longer a signal of a clean history.

The era of default-public everything on Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter is behind us. What the subject shared publicly in 2014 has been auto-privatised — sometimes by the subject, sometimes by the platform on a policy change — and the current view is not the view a 2019 investigator would have had.
section.subtitle: Before you look
section.p: Some subjects who did the work to disappear had a reason. An abuse survivor. A protected witness. A former activist under a régime that still remembers their name. A parent estranged from a violent partner. A whistleblower whose employer would still enjoy finding them.

You will not always know which of those apply to the subject on your desk. The safe assumption is that a subject who defended thoroughly and quietly — who compartmentalised across identities rather than merely stripped a profile — probably did so because they had a reason, and the reason may still exist. That is a signal for you, not a licence.

The engagement scope is where the ethical question sits. If the client's legitimate purpose is answered by the record you can access without pushing through a defence, answer it and stop. If it is not — if the client is asking a question that only surfaces after you push — that is where you go back to the client, name what you have hit, and let counsel decide whether the engagement continues. You do not push through a defence just because you can. You especially do not push through a defence because it is interesting.
The competent subject is not always your adversary. Sometimes they are a witness whose safety was the entire point of the wall. Read the wall before you touch the bricks.
section.subtitle: The method, step by step
section.p: Step 1 — Map before you defend, if you are the defender. (Defender's chair.) The self-audit runs the same passes you would run against a subject: WHOIS on every domain you have ever registered, CT-log search on every domain and every wildcard, historical WHOIS lookups, image search on every profile photograph you have ever uploaded, an archive search on your professional handle. You do this every six to twelve months. What you find is the door you would have left open if you had not looked.

Step 2 — Compartmentalise identities before you clean. (Defender's chair.) One email per purpose is the rule. professional@, newsletters@, financial@, family@ — each in a separate account with a separate password, each behind a mail forwarder if the identity is a public one. One phone number per identity, or a VoIP number for the identities that do not need a personal one. The point is not secrecy. The point is that a leak on one identity does not cross to another.

Step 3 — Do the domain hygiene properly. (Defender's chair.) Privacy-protected WHOIS on every domain. Name-servers that do not carry your customer identity in their hostnames. CAA records that scope certificate issuance to a single CA. Certificates issued only for the hostnames you actually publish, so a wildcard does not seed a CT log with every internal subdomain you own. security.txt and humans.txt present only if you are willing to have them read. Assume every certificate you have ever issued is in a CT log forever; publish accordingly.

Step 4 — Photograph hygiene, and its limits. (Both chairs.) Strip EXIF from every uploaded photograph. Consider whether the photograph itself needs a face — a subject who does not want to be facesearched should not publish a front-facing headshot on the primary handle. Understand the limit: background triangulation still works. A photograph with the face obscured and the venue visible tells an investigator with a satellite view where the photograph was taken. The competent defender knows this and either omits the photograph or crops out the background before uploading.

p.emphasis: From the investigator's chair, this is where you keep working. If a subject has stripped EXIF and obscured the face, the background is still yours to read. Building silhouettes against a skyline, a distinctive railing, a plaza with a public monument — these are all in the frame the subject sent. Half the geolocation work you already know still applies.

section.p: Step 5 — Social-graph hygiene, from both sides. (Both chairs.) A private profile leaks through everyone else's public one. A friend tagged you in a photograph. A colleague reacted to your comment on a post that was public. A former employee wrote a leaving-post that named you. As a defender you cannot control your entire graph, but you can ask the two or three people closest to you not to tag you and can un-tag yourself from what already exists. As an investigator you already know to work the graph outward from the subject; when the subject is private, the graph is the whole engagement.

cite.p: Try it (2026). Take your own primary professional handle. Run it, verbatim, through the Wayback Machine, one archive-org variant search on the handle string, and one CT-log search on any personal domain you own. Do the pass without cleaning up first. Write down every one of your own real-world identifiers that surfaces in the first hour: a personal email, a phone number, an old employer's internal subdomain, a photograph you thought was down. That list is your closed-door checklist. The next six weekends are how you close each door — the same way you would advise a client to.

section.p: Step 6 — Text-fingerprint hygiene. (Defender's chair, painfully.) The unavoidable one. Cadence, sentence length, favourite punctuation, the parenthetical habit, the em-dash, the specific way you open a paragraph — these survive a change of handle. A subject who changes their public name but continues to write the same way is identifiable by a competent stylistic-analysis pass. There is no full defence against this. The partial defence is to write differently in different contexts, deliberately and consistently, which almost no-one has the discipline for. The realistic defence is to accept that if someone with enough time reads enough of your writing across enough handles, the writing will link the handles for them.

Step 7 — Fossils and historical archives. (Investigator's chair.) When the current record is closed, the historical record is where you go. The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine holds copies of pages that the subject took down. The archive.today mirror holds copies of pages the Wayback Machine never captured.
