p.emphasis: The clause names what is bought, what is not, and when it is due. The out-of-scope block is longer than the in-scope block for the same reason Chapter 5 gave: it is the part counsel will read first if the candidate ever writes.

section.p: Salmi signs at 14:02. The retainer clears at 14:38. You open a case folder named 2026-05-MC-Whitcombe, initialise the log with the day's clock check against pool.ntp.org — offset 0.19s — and write the first log line: Retainer signed 14:02 CET; scope as attached; deliverable Thursday 18:00 CET. Chapter 3 is now running underneath everything. Every artefact from this point in the week onward goes into the case file with a URL in every form the target uses, a UTC capture time, a SHA-256 of the bytes fetched, two independent preservation copies, and a one-line intent entry naming why you went looking.
You do not touch the record yet. It is Monday afternoon. Tuesday is early enough.
section.subtitle: Tuesday — the record
section.p: You start at 08:15 with a clean research browser profile — no personal cookies, no logged-in Google, no autofill. The three handles Salmi sent are on the desk in front of you and you work them in the boring order Volume 1 taught you. LinkedIn first, because it is where the résumé claim lives. GitHub second, because it will either self-link to the LinkedIn or it will not, and either way that is a finding. The personal site third, because personal sites almost always leak more than their owners meant them to.
By lunchtime you have five things in the notes.

• The LinkedIn profile at linkedin.com/in/jarrah-whitcombe-6641 — snapshot arch-2026-05-12-0847Z-4d1a, capture 2026-05-12T08:47:11Z, artefact SHA-256 c9e1… — carries the two roles Salmi's résumé listed, in the same date ranges, and lists three prior roles she did not send you. All three are inside the same Adelaide research ecosystem and all three are consistent with a materials-science career of that length.

• The GitHub account jwhitcombe-materials — snapshot arch-2026-05-12-0912Z-1e77 — has a bio field that reads Materials scientist. Ostrava. Personal projects only. See whitcombe-materials.example.net. The self-link to the personal site is on the page. That closes the first identity attribution at strong, on the self-link and the reused profile photograph across LinkedIn, GitHub, and the ICMC-2024 speaker page.

• The personal site at whitcombe-materials.example.net — snapshot arch-2026-05-12-0938Z-2b03 — is a static portfolio with three sections and a contact form. The WHOIS is behind a privacy service, which is not a finding by itself; almost every professional's personal domain in 2026 is. The DNS points at a boilerplate hosting provider you have seen a thousand times.

• The ICMC-2024 speaker page — snapshot arch-2026-05-12-1001Z-9f42 — carries the same photograph, a two-hundred-word bio matching the résumé's roles at Larsen-Voss and Kelso, and a talk title on ceramic-matrix composites for high-temperature abrasion.

• The Kelso Advanced Coatings archive — the firm was acquired by a larger group in 2019 and its public site is thin — has three press-release mentions of Whitcombe by name across 2013–2017, all consistent with the résumé claim.

By early afternoon you have gone looking for what is not there. Chapter 6 says a competent subject in 2026 has already closed the obvious doors, and Whitcombe has closed two. There is no visible Facebook or Instagram footprint under any of the plausible handle variants. There is no personal Twitter/X account. The GitHub is scoped to personal projects and every repository is a materials-science calculation notebook, not a professional history reveal. He is not hiding — he is compartmentalised. That is what competent looks like now.
You draft the shape of the report on Tuesday evening at 17:40. Four candidate findings in your notes.
• W-F1. Identity attribution across the three handles and the ICMC speaker page — strong, on the self-link and the reused photograph.
• W-F2. The résumé's professional history at Larsen-Voss and Kelso is corroborated by the public record — strong, on the LinkedIn snapshot, the ICMC bio, and the Kelso press-release archive.
• W-F3. No visible undisclosed conflicts on the surface record — moderate, because absence of surface signal is not absence of conflict, and the report will need to say so.
• W-F4. Compartmentalisation pattern consistent with a candidate who has been in the field long enough to know how the record reads — noted, not a finding of concern in itself.
You close the log at 18:12. You go home. You expect Wednesday to be a quiet day of provenance work and a peer read booked for Thursday morning.
section.subtitle: Wednesday — the peer read that changes it
section.p: At 09:47 the junior on your team — call him Erez, on the desk beside yours, three months into a two-year contract — walks over with a printout of the ICMC-2024 speaker page and puts it on the corner of your desk. He does not sit down. The bio at the bottom mentions a board seat, he says. At an Australian materials-testing consortium called ATMC-Southern. Is that in the résumé.

You look. The bio's last sentence, which you read on Tuesday and did not underline, reads Currently serving on the technical advisory board of the Australian Testing Materials Consortium — Southern Region. It is not in the résumé Salmi sent. Board seats are supposed to be in the résumé. They are supposed to be in the résumé specifically because the scope document names them.

Your first reflex, at 09:48, is to tell Erez the bio is out of date — that a conference bio written in early 2024 would have carried a board seat he then rolled off — and to move on. You almost do. What stops you is Chapter 8. The junior spotted something. Even if he is wrong, the correct move is to check, not to explain. You tell him to find out when Whitcombe rolled off the board, if he did, and to bring you the sourcing.

He is back at 11:16 with three things. The ATMC-Southern board page, live and current at atmc-southern.example.org/about/board, snapshot arch-2026-05-13-1108Z-6a11, carries Whitcombe as a sitting board member as of the capture. A Wayback snapshot from 2023-11-04 carries him. A Wayback snapshot from 2022-06-18 does not. The board seat began between June 2022 and November 2023 and, on the public record as it stands Wednesday morning, he is still on it.

That is the first thing. The second thing is what the ATMC-Southern board actually does. It is not a materials-testing hobby group. It is the entity that certifies the abrasion-resistance ratings that Australian and New Zealand regulators require for industrial-abrasive imports. Which raises the second question, and this is where you stop reading the printout and open your own weekly-scans pipeline — the Chapter 7 pipeline that watches domain registrations and corporate filings against your standing client watchlist. You already have a signal in it. Meridian Carbide's Rotterdam parent group — Ostrom Holdings BV — filed a notice in the Netherlands corporate register on 2026-03-11 announcing the completion of the acquisition of a firm called Karratha Industrial Coatings, an Australian subsidiary of a firm ATMC-Southern certifies twice a year.

You sit with that for ten minutes. Then you open the case file and write a new log line at 11:31. Potential conflict-of-interest: subject holds sitting board seat at ATMC-Southern, the certifying body for Karratha Industrial Coatings, which the client's parent group acquired 2026-03-11. Overlap window: subject's board tenure began between 2022-06 and 2023-11 and is current. Independent of the vetting question. Material to disclosure.

The COI is not disqualifying. Whitcombe did not sit on the ATMC-Southern board because of the Karratha acquisition — the board seat predates it by at least eighteen months. He did not fail to disclose a role he had taken for the parent group. But he is being hired into the Head of Materials role at a subsidiary of a group that just acquired a firm certified by a body he sits on. That is the kind of overlap counsel writes a paragraph about in the offer letter, not the kind that kills a hire.

The archive fossil that lets you catch it is the Wayback snapshot of the ATMC-Southern board page from 2022 — a page that no longer surfaces in an ordinary search because the current version is what the search index returns. Chapter 6 called this the discipline of pulling archived versions of a subject's adjacent-institution pages, not only the subject's own. You had not run that pull yet on Tuesday. Erez ran it Wednesday morning because he saw one sentence in a bio you had already read.

At 13:20 you book a peer read for Thursday morning at 10:00 with Ines, the peer who owes you a read and to whom you owe two. You send her the case file as it stands and one paragraph naming the COI question. You spend the rest of Wednesday afternoon closing the provenance around the COI — every ATMC-Southern snapshot hashed, the Netherlands corporate-register notice preserved on Perma.cc and archive.today, the acquisition date corroborated against a public press release. You go home at 18:40 with three findings from Tuesday and one new material finding you did not have twenty-four hours ago.
You also throw out the summary you were going to draft Wednesday evening. Chapter 4 was right: the summary gets rewritten last.
section.subtitle: Thursday — writing the report
section.p: Ines reads the draft at 10:00. She does two things. She kills one of Tuesday's findings and confirms the COI.

The finding she kills is W-F4 — the compartmentalisation note. Not because it is wrong, but because it is an observation about the shape of the record, not a finding about the subject, and a decision-grade report does not carry the investigator's opinion of the subject's operational hygiene. It goes into the limitations section as one sentence: the subject's public presence is consistent with a professional who has curated his surface record; the record checked does not surface material a curated presence would omit.

The COI she confirms at strong. Three independent signals: the ATMC-Southern board page live and archived, the Netherlands corporate-register notice of the Karratha acquisition, and Whitcombe's own signed disclosure on the ATMC-Southern board page listing his employer as Larsen-Voss (not Meridian Carbide, because he does not work there yet, but the disclosure form on the ATMC-Southern page is the one that will need updating on the day he signs). Ines writes one sentence in the margin. If counsel does nothing else with this report, they need to see this paragraph before they see anything else. You underline it.

You draft the summary between 11:30 and 13:00 and rewrite it twice. You cut a paragraph you were fond of about the coherence of the professional record because it is the paragraph that would let a reader stop reading before they reached the COI paragraph. You lead with the COI. You put the professional-history corroboration second. You put the identity attribution third. The recommendation line is one sentence: the record supports proceeding, provided the offer letter carries disclosure and recusal language addressing the ATMC-Southern board seat. The report goes to Salmi at 17:22 Thursday. Thirty-eight minutes early.

The report anatomy is the one from Chapter 4. Five sections. Scope recap in two sentences. Summary of findings with a confidence line per finding, under two hundred words. Findings in detail with provenance inline. What was ruled out — the compartmentalisation note, the initial reflex that the ICMC bio was out of date, an inference that the personal site's DNS pointed at anything unusual. Limitations — what a competent counter-investigator would have closed that Whitcombe has not tried to close, and what a follow-up read in six months could still surface. The COI finding paragraph reads, in the finished draft, like this.
section.subtitle: mini-report excerpt: finding W-F4 (COI)

p.code: Whitcombe holds a current seat on the technical advisory
is the certifying body for Karratha Industrial Coatings,
which the Client's parent group, Ostrom Holdings BV,
predates the acquisition and is not disclosed in the
résumé provided to the Client. Confidence: strong, on
three independent signals. Recommendation: material to
disclosure; the offer letter should address recusal.

p.emphasis: Ninety-two words. One finding, one confidence rung, three provenance references, one recommendation. Written in the sentence you would be willing to read back in a deposition.

section.p: Nothing in the report goes further than the case file. Nothing in the report speculates about whether Whitcombe should have disclosed the board seat in the résumé, whether the omission was intentional, or whether his conduct on the ATMC-Southern board has been anything other than routine. The report says what the record shows. Counsel decides what to do about it.

You close the log at 17:48 with the day's last line. Report sent to Client 17:22 CET; case file frozen at path 2026-05-MC-Whitcombe/case-2026-05-14-final; all artefacts hashed; peer read complete. You go home. It is Thursday evening. You do not know yet what will happen on Friday, and if you have written the report correctly, what happens on Friday does not depend on you.
section.subtitle: Friday — the report lands
section.p: Salmi forwards the report to counsel at 07:41 Friday. Counsel — a partner at a mid-sized Rotterdam firm who has read your work for Meridian Carbide before — prints it, reads the summary and the ruled-out section standing at the printer, and gets to the COI paragraph on the second page. She calls the CEO at 09:03. The call takes twelve minutes. The outcome — you learn this from Salmi's note in the case file two months later — is a rewrite of the offer letter. Counsel drafts the new paragraph over lunch.

The new paragraph in the offer letter names the ATMC-Southern board seat, requires Whitcombe to notify the board of his new employment within thirty days of start, requires him to recuse from any ATMC-Southern proceeding involving Karratha Industrial Coatings or any other Ostrom Holdings subsidiary for the duration of his employment, and requires an annual written disclosure to Meridian Carbide's own compliance officer. The offer letter goes to Whitcombe at 16:15 Friday. He reads it over the weekend. He signs on Monday. The hire proceeds.
section.subtitle: The two weeks after
section.p: You do not hear from Salmi. Not on Friday, not the following week, not the week after that. On Monday two weeks later at 11:03 an automated notification from your invoicing system tells you Meridian Carbide has paid the engagement invoice. Nothing else. No thank-you note. No debrief call. No forwarded copy of the signed offer letter. You look at the notification for about three seconds and go back to the engagement you are on. That is the whole reward.
section.subtitle: What the engagement taught
section.p: The shape of the week is durable. Every case you take from here rearranges the specifics — a different subject, a different mid-week surprise, a different paragraph in a different offer letter — but the shape holds. Monday holds the acceptance and the letter. Tuesday holds the record. Wednesday is where the report you were about to write gets rewritten. Thursday writes the report. Friday hands it off. That is not a coincidence; it is a working week with a scope document at the top of it.

The report is the product. Not the investigation. Not the notes. Not the fact that you found the board seat. The product is a document counsel could act on in five minutes and did. Everything you did on Monday and Tuesday and Wednesday existed so that the sentence on the page Thursday afternoon could carry a rung and a source and a recommendation without a single word going further than the record. If the report had said appears to hold a board seat instead of holds a current seat, on three independent signals, counsel would have called you at 09:30 Friday to ask what you meant, and the offer letter would have gone out unchanged.

The team is the difference. Erez saw the sentence in the ICMC bio you had already read. Ines killed the finding you were about to over-write. Neither of them was doing your job for you. Both of them were doing the job the discipline of a peer read exists for. A solo investigator would have shipped a report on Thursday that did not carry the COI paragraph, and it would still have been a competent report — and it would have missed the paragraph that made the offer letter defensible. The team is not a luxury. It is the design margin on the report.

The ethics are the frame. Nothing in the engagement asked you to look at Whitcombe's private life, and nothing in the report does. Nothing in the engagement asked you to judge whether he should have disclosed the board seat in the résumé, and nothing in the report does. The scope was written down on Monday and the report Thursday sits inside it. That is not an accident; that is Chapter 1 at the top of the week and Chapter 5 in the middle of it. The mess — the fossil archive, the junior's observation, the summary you threw out Wednesday night — is the job. It is not a sign that you did anything wrong. It is what the shape is designed to hold.

This week is one week. There are twenty-five years' worth of them ahead of you, and the shape is what you carry between them. Every engagement rearranges the specifics; the acceptance decision on Monday, the record on Tuesday, the peer read that changes it on Wednesday, the report Thursday, the silence after Friday — those hold. The four books were about learning the shape. The rest of the career is the shape, one week at a time.
section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • A working engagement is a week shape: acceptance on Monday, scope on Monday, record on Tuesday, peer read on Wednesday or Thursday, report on Thursday, hand-off on Friday, silence after.
• The acceptance decision is a real decision — practice the ten-minute pause on engagements that do not need it, so you have the reflex on the one that does.
• The scope document is written before the retainer clears; the out-of-scope block is longer than the in-scope block because it is the section counsel will read first if the subject ever writes.
• Every artefact goes into the case file at capture — URL, UTC, SHA-256, two preservation copies, one-line intent — because you cannot back-fill a chain of custody.
• The mid-week finding that changes the report almost always comes from a peer read or an archive fossil, and almost always from a sentence you had already read and not underlined.
• The COI paragraph goes to counsel exactly as strong as the evidence supports, with three provenance references on the page, and does not editorialise about the subject.
• The report is the product; the finding is what happens to fit inside it; the invoice-paid confirmation two weeks later is the whole reward.
section.subtitle: What comes next
section.p: The epilogue. The end of the course.

p.emphasis: Four volumes, one method, twenty-five years ahead of you.

section.p: Stop for a second and look at where you are standing.

Four years ago — if you started with Volume 1 the day it came out — you were somebody who wanted to know how the world of open records worked. You pulled a first thread. You learned the shape of a loop. You learned to read a person out of a scatter of platforms. You learned to read the buried places, the deleted ones, the certificate logs, the misconfigured origin. And in this book, you learned how to turn all of that into a craft — a report a lawyer can act on, an engagement a client can pay for, a peer read that catches your sentence before counsel does, a chain of custody that survives eighteen months in a case file.
Four books. One method. And the method is now yours in a way it was not before.
section.subtitle: What you can do now
section.p: You can take a Monday-morning message from an HR director and know, by lunchtime, whether the scope you have been offered is one you can accept. You can write an engagement letter in a paragraph and a clause. You can move through a record with the ladder in your head — weak, moderate, strong, confirmed — and mean each rung when you place it. You can produce an artefact a lawyer will read in five minutes and act on in ten. You can hit a subject who defended against exactly what you were about to try, and know what still surfaces and what does not. You can build automation that does not silently rot. You can name the four people you need around you and know where the gaps are. You can walk into an engagement on Monday and out of it on Friday with the client's counsel using your report the way you meant it to be used.
That is a working professional. That is what this course was for.
section.subtitle: The method is bigger than the method
section.p: There is something the four books do not say out loud, and you have already begun to feel it. The specific pivots are perishable. The specific tools will be gone. The specific platforms named on these pages will merge, die, get bought, get regulated, get replaced. Half the URLs you underlined in Volume 1 no longer resolve. That is not a failure of the book; that is the tempo of the field.

What is durable is the shape. The loop. The ladder. The independence of signals. The self-link over the stack. The scope you wrote down before you looked. The provenance you captured at the moment of capture. The peer who reads your draft before counsel does. The stop-sign you put in front of yourself when the pivot would have taken you across a line you signed. Those are the same in 2026 as they will be in 2046. The tools change; the shape does not.

If you leave these four books with one belief, let it be that. Shape is durable. Tools are disposable. Every new platform you meet, every new signal you learn to read, every new rate-limit that slams shut in your face — the shape tells you what to do next.
section.subtitle: The next twenty-five years
section.p: You are not at the end of anything. You are at the point where the training wheels come off and the actual career begins.

The next twenty-five years of your working life will be spent inside this method, watching it get stretched by cases that do not fit any of the templates in Appendix B. You will train a junior who becomes better than you. You will get a peer whose read makes your work sharper for a decade. You will meet a client whose engagement teaches you something you did not know these four books had failed to teach you, and you will write a new chapter for yourself. You will decline engagements you would have taken at thirty and take engagements you would have declined at forty. You will develop opinions on things this book was silent about, and you will be right about most of them.

You will also, occasionally, make a mistake that a Volume 4 reader should not have made. You will hedge a strong finding as confirmed under deadline pressure and get the call from counsel at 08:10 on a Friday. You will let a scope drift on a client you liked. You will follow a pivot that felt clean and turn out to have crossed a line you were tired enough not to see. The professional is not the one who never makes those mistakes. The professional is the one who names them in the notes, brings them to a peer, and does not make the same one twice.
section.subtitle: What this book is not
section.p: There is no Volume 5 coming. This course closes here. Not because the field is finished — the field is only accelerating — but because everything that comes after Volume 4 is not book-shaped. It is casework. It is a peer group. It is a mentor you trust. It is a bad Friday afternoon that teaches you what a chapter never could. Some of you will write your own books; some of you will teach a course of your own; some of you will do the work quietly for a career and never publish a word. All three are correct answers.

If you want to keep in touch, keep in touch. If you find something the books got wrong, tell me. If you build something on top of the method, show me. I have been in this field long enough to know that the best students eventually correct the teacher — and I am counting on you to be one of them.
section.subtitle: The last word
section.p: Every shadow has a name. You already know how to find it. What the four books tried to teach you, in the end, was when not to. The professional is the one who knows where to stop — and now that the course is closed, that discipline is yours to keep sharp on your own, one engagement at a time.
Go do the work.
— Yehor

p.emphasis: The shapes of tools a working professional keeps in reach, and the ones that changed since Volume 3.

section.p: Volume 3's Appendix A named the working shapes of tools for buried records. This one is the professional's kit — the same shapes, plus the ones a paid engagement needs: case management, custody, billing, legal-frame lookup, redaction, peer review, and a small automation stack that does not rot.
Everything below is a shape, not an endorsement. Specific vendors change every eighteen months. The shape is what carries.
section.subtitle: Case management
section.p: • Case file structure. One directory per engagement. Inside: 01_engagement_letter/, 02_scope/, 03_raw_captures/, 04_notes/, 05_findings/, 06_report_drafts/, 07_final_report/, 08_correspondence/, 09_provenance_log.md. Not sophisticated. Sophisticated is what rots. A boring layout survives handovers, audits, and eight-year discovery requests.

• Case-management tools. i2 Analyst's Notebook, Nuix Investigate, and Maltego Enterprise sit at one end (heavy, expensive, licensed). Notion and Obsidian sit at the other (light, cheap, DIY). Between them: BlackDot Solutions Videris, Bright Data's investigation stack, and a growing crop of open-source case managers built on top of Aleph or DocumentCloud. Pick one and stay with it for a year; switching mid-caseload is where evidence gets lost.
• The rule. The tool that survives is the one you actually update on Wednesday afternoon at 16:20, not the one that looked good in the demo.
section.subtitle: Provenance and custody
section.p: • Archive-on-capture services. Wayback (web.archive.org), archive.today, Perma.cc (built for law-review citation; useful for legal work), Conifer (formerly WebRecorder — full-fidelity captures with authenticated sessions where scope permits). Capture to at least two of these on anything material.

• Local capture tools. SingleFile (browser extension, produces a single self-contained HTML that hashes cleanly), Hunchly (subscription; case-linked capture with automatic hashing and timeline), Fireshot for wider screenshots.
• Hashing. sha256sum from the command line, or the hashlib module in Python. Any digest tool works if you record which one you used; SHA-256 is the accepted standard for the next decade.

• Signing the log. Hash-chained JSONL log, one line per artefact, each line carrying the SHA-256 of the previous line. Chapter 3 covers the shape. A cryptographic signature over each day's log tail turns the file into evidence.
section.subtitle: Reporting and redaction
section.p: • Report drafting. Markdown or LaTeX for maintainable source; Word for delivery to counsel who edit in Track Changes. Never PDF as a source format — you cannot edit a PDF cleanly, and every round of edits by counsel will introduce artefacts.

• Redaction (for shared or exhibits versions). Adobe Acrobat's redact-and-flatten workflow, or pdftk plus qpdf if you like the command line. Never redact by drawing a black box in a viewer — the text under the box is still in the file.
• Version control on drafts. Git, private repo, no exceptions. Ten years of drafts in a directory with _final_final_v3 in the filename is not archiving; it is chaos.
section.subtitle: Legal-frame lookup
section.p: • Live-law reference works. For FCRA (US pre-employment): the CFPB's current guidance and the Fair Credit Reporting Act itself at www.consumer.ftc.gov. For GDPR: the EDPB's guidelines index. For the UK: the ICO's guides on investigative processing and Article 6(1)(f) legitimate interest.

• Jurisdictional lookup. DLA Piper's Data Protection Laws of the World is a working reference (free-tier online). Bird & Bird's GDPR tracker. The IAPP's regulatory tracker for the newer state privacy laws (California CPRA, Virginia VCDPA, Colorado CPA, etc.).

• The rule. You do not practise law. You maintain enough live-law literacy to know when to call counsel. The books above are not a substitute for counsel; they are a checklist that tells you when to reach for one.
section.subtitle: Automation stack
section.p: • Language. Python (stdlib + requests + beautifulsoup4 + polars + hashlib + python-whois) covers 95% of what a working professional needs. Node.js if the ecosystem forces your hand. Bash for glue.
• Versioning. Git. Every tool you ship carries its own semver string in its output. Chapter 7 covers the shape.

• Scheduling. Cron on a small Linux box you own, or a workflow orchestrator (Prefect, Dagster) if you have grown to more than a handful of pipelines. Do not schedule critical monitoring on your laptop — laptops close.

• Monitoring. Healthchecks.io (or self-hosted equivalent) — every scheduled job pings a URL when it succeeds; if the ping is late, you get an email. This one line of instrumentation catches ninety percent of silent-rot failures.
• Secrets. Never in the git repo. .env files locally, a proper secrets manager (Doppler, 1Password Secrets Automation, HashiCorp Vault) once the surface justifies it.
section.subtitle: Communications and OPSEC
section.p: • Client communication. Signal for casual coordination; email for anything that needs to be discoverable. ProtonMail or Tuta if the client is comfortable; regular corporate email otherwise. Never Telegram for client work — its DM privacy model is not what most clients think it is.

• Case-specific mail forwarders. Fastmail masked addresses, SimpleLogin, or a mycasename@yourdomain.com alias per engagement. Compartmentalises correspondence and gives you a clean shutdown when the engagement closes.
• Encrypted drives. VeraCrypt on Windows/Linux; the built-in FileVault on macOS. Full-disk encryption on any laptop that leaves the office.
• The clean research browser. Chapter 8 covers it. A profile with no cookies, no sync, no extensions you did not choose. One per engagement is best; one per year at minimum.
section.subtitle: Peer-review and quality tools
section.p: • Peer-review checklist. See Appendix B for the template. A checklist is not a formality — it is what makes the peer read repeatable.
• Timer. A physical kitchen timer or a phone timer. Peer reads are time-boxed (40 minutes is a working default). Without a timer they either run long, or get skipped.
• Track Changes / diff tools. For document-level peer review: Word's Track Changes, or git diff --word-diff if the peer is technical. Peer comments should be visible in the draft, not remembered.
section.subtitle: Billing and business
section.p: • Invoicing. FreshBooks, Wave, or a self-hosted Invoice Ninja. Do not run a professional practice on ad-hoc PDFs.
• Time tracking. Toggl, Harvest, or a plain-text ledger. Every engagement has an authorised hours ceiling; without a timer you will exceed it silently.

• Retainer / trust account. In jurisdictions that require it, keep client retainer funds in a separate account from operating funds. Talk to an accountant before you take your first paid engagement, not after.
section.subtitle: What died since Volume 3
section.p: • Google's cache: operator. Fully retired.
• Microsoft's Defender Threat Intelligence portal (the old RiskIQ properties). Migrated into Sentinel; standalone free tier gone.
• Twitter/X advanced search for handle-history lookups. Post-2023 rate-limits and API changes make this brittle for professional work; treat any handle-history claim from X as moderate at best.
• Free-tier Farsight DNSDB. Enterprise-only now; SecurityTrails and VirusTotal Enterprise cover most of the same shape.
• Wayback Machine's changes tool — still exists, but Wayback's own coverage of major platforms has narrowed under legal pressure. Cross-capture to archive.today for anything material.
section.subtitle: A note on cost
section.p: A professional toolbox is a line item, not a personal expense. The moment you take a paying engagement, the cost of the vendors that engagement required goes on the invoice — as a pass-through, or as an overhead line, or as a specific tool-cost item. A hobbyist works out of the free tier; a professional works out of the tools the engagement needs and passes the cost through with a clear line on the bill.

The exception: personal-safety and pro-bono work — safeguarding, missing persons, journalism under legal threat. Some vendors offer public-interest tiers; the ones that do not, you fund out of the same pool as any other charitable expense. Do not resent the cost of the tool a real case needs.

p.emphasis: Six documents a working engagement needs. Edit before use; do not copy blindly.

section.p: Every template below is a starting point. Every jurisdiction, every client type, every engagement shape changes at least one clause. Read every clause with the client's counsel before signing anything. The templates are professional shortcuts, not legal advice.
Names, firms, and identifiers throughout are fictional.
section.subtitle: 1. Engagement letter (short form)

p.emphasis: The lines a paid investigator crosses only by mistake — and never twice.

section.p: The Volume 3 Red Lines still hold. Read that card first if you have not in a while. This one adds the lines that only appear once you are being paid, only once a client has authority over a scope, only once a report leaves your hands and lands with counsel.
Nothing here is a legal defence. Every jurisdiction adds more. Read every one at the start of every case; the reading takes a minute; it saves careers.
section.subtitle: Engagement acceptance
section.p: • The scope is a clause, not a mood. If you cannot write down in a paragraph what you have been retained to do and what you have not, do not accept the engagement. A retroactive "we understood it to include" is what depositions are made of.

• Refuse engagements whose question is not answerable inside the frame. A client who wants you to answer is the candidate hiding something? is asking for a blank cheque. The professional turns that into does the public record surface material undisclosed to the client, in the categories the engagement letter names? If the client will not accept the reframe, the engagement is not one you take.

• Refuse engagements aimed at a person the client does not have authority over. Family members of a subject, journalists, whistleblowers, former partners in a domestic dispute — no client has the standing to authorise an investigation of these people. A vetting engagement about a candidate is not a vetting engagement about the candidate's spouse.

• The client is not your only stakeholder. The subject has interests you must not harm even where the client wishes you would. Counsel has interests in an accurate, defensible report. A regulator, eighteen months from now, has interests in seeing your work stand up. Serve all three.
section.subtitle: The frame
section.p: • Never report a finding the frame forbids you to report, even if you saw it. Religious affiliation, sexual orientation, pregnancy, health status, protected-class membership. You will sometimes see these signals in the record. The report is silent on them. Counsel is told by phone that the section is silent and, if the finding is material, that a conversation about scope needs to happen. Nothing goes in writing that the frame forbids.

• Adverse-action law is not optional. In pre-hire vetting under FCRA and its equivalents, the client's adverse-action procedure is triggered by findings in your report. If the client will not commit to running the adverse-action process, the engagement is not one you take.

• You do not practise law. You maintain enough live-law literacy to know when to call counsel. The moment a scope question depends on how a statute is interpreted, that is a counsel question, not yours.
section.subtitle: Data and custody
section.p: • You do not touch a login. Volume 1 through 4 unchanged. A paid engagement does not create a legal basis you did not have; the engagement letter cannot authorise you to break the law.

• Breach data is a source, not a credential. You may cite a breach as evidence that an account existed; you may not use the credentials in it to access anything. A breach is a snapshot of an event. It is not a key. And it is not universally lawful to possess. In several EU member states, hosting or re-deriving a breach corpus is criminalised as computer misuse or as unlawful processing of Article 9/10 data under GDPR; in the UK, the Computer Misuse Act and the DPA 2018 impose parallel constraints; in the US, some breach corpora are covered by consent decrees and DOJ guidance. Consult counsel before you ingest any breach corpus into a case file. Never mirror one to your own storage. Never keep one inside an engagement folder. Where a client's engagement requires you to check a breach, do so through an authorised service (a paid API to a service that has taken the licensing question on) rather than by holding the corpus.

• Data-subject access requests (DSAR / SAR) reach the investigator, not only the client. In the EU under GDPR Article 15 and in the UK under the DPA 2018, a subject of an investigation is entitled to ask you — the investigator — what personal data of theirs you hold, why, on what lawful basis, and to whom you disclosed it. The client's engagement letter does not extinguish that right. Have a process for it: a designated contact, a written response template, a defined thirty-day response window, and a policy for the narrow exemptions (litigation privilege, ongoing investigation) that require counsel's read before you claim them. A DSAR served on a solo investigator with no process is a career event; a DSAR served on a shop with a process is a form.

• Every artefact enters the case file with a hash and a timestamp at the moment of capture. Not the next day, not before you leave for lunch, not after you have "cleaned up" the notes. At capture. Chapter 3 covers the shape.

• Retention has an end date. The case file has a retention period named in the engagement letter. When the period is up, the file is destroyed to a documented standard, and the destruction itself is logged. A permanent archive of every case you have ever worked is not a filing system; it is a liability.
section.subtitle: The report
section.p: • Every sentence is a sentence you would read back in a deposition. Chapter 4 covers the discipline. If any word goes further than the evidence, cut the word.
• You do not editorialise the subject. Facts about the record are findings. Judgements about the subject's character or choices are opinions and do not belong in a decision-grade report.

• You do not include material outside scope, even if it is interesting, even if it is embarrassing to the subject, even if the client would like you to. The report is what the engagement letter promised. Everything else is your own notes.
• You do not deliver findings you cannot defend to a peer. A peer read is a professional gate, not a formality. A draft that has not passed peer review is not a report.
section.subtitle: Team and referral
section.p: • You do not permit a junior to sign a report they did not fully understand. Signature is authorship; authorship is responsibility. A junior contributes; the senior signs.

• You do not accept work outside your competence and quietly outsource it. If part of the engagement needs a partner firm — physical surveillance, forensic imaging, foreign-jurisdiction records — the partner firm is named in the engagement letter or in a documented amendment, and their deliverable carries their own signature.

• You do not refer to a partner firm you would not use yourself. A referral is an endorsement in the eyes of the client. Referring to a firm to save a bad relationship, save a fee, or save a difficult conversation is a red line.
section.subtitle: Money
section.p: • You do not accept an engagement whose fee incentivises a specific finding. A contingency arrangement — "you get paid more if the finding is X" — is a red line in this profession. The retainer buys your attention, not your conclusion.

• You do not accept payment structures that hide the client. If the counterparty on the invoice is not the client named in the engagement letter, and the difference is not explained by a documented corporate structure, walk. Money laundering and reputational proxy work look very similar on the paperwork.

• Discovery is a real cost. If the case file may be discoverable in litigation eighteen months from now, the engagement letter says so, and the client's counsel understands. Building a case file that pretends discovery cannot happen is not a discipline; it is a fantasy that fails at the first subpoena.
section.subtitle: The line you cannot outsource
section.p: Above every rule: the professional is the one who knows when to stop. The paid version of that is the professional is the one who knows when to decline. Learning when to walk away from an engagement is the single hardest discipline this book asks of you, and the one that separates a working career from a short one.
Read this card at the start of every engagement. Every one. It takes a minute. It saves careers.

title.p: Appendix D — Take It Back (The Consultant's Perimeter)

p.emphasis: Your own footprint, closed against the version of you a competent adversary would build.

section.p: Volume 3's Take It Back asked you to close your own footprint against a professional adversary. This one is the consultant's version — a working investigator has a larger footprint than a private person, because you are visible as a service, because your clients are visible as clients (whether or not they meant to be), and because a competent counter-investigator will now look at YOU exactly the way you look at your subjects.
Do this checklist twice a year. Do it once immediately after every case that made the news, however tangentially.
section.subtitle: Your professional presence
section.p: • Search your own name. Every alias you have ever used professionally. LinkedIn, personal blog, firm website, speaker bios at conferences you attended, quoted appearances in press, expert-witness registers if you have testified. Read what a subject's counsel would read.

• Read your own case fingerprints. Papers you co-authored. Talks you gave that named a technique. Threads you posted on public forums. Every one of these is a signature that ties you to a class of case, and thus to a class of subject.

• Redact what does not need to be there. A talk you gave in 2019 that named a case study is a talk that ties you to that case class forever. Ask yourself whether the visibility still pays for the exposure.
section.subtitle: Your firm's presence
section.p: • Read your firm's WHOIS and CT logs the way you read a subject's. Every staging domain your firm has ever spun up is in CT forever. A dev.casefile.yourfirm.com in a CT log is telling any adversary the shape of your internal tooling. Close subdomains you do not need; move truly internal ones to a private CA.

• Read your firm's public writeups. Case studies on your website. Anonymised examples in a marketing deck. The pattern of anonymisation itself is a signature — if you always change the industry to "logistics", a real logistics case will stand out. Rotate the anonymisation shape.

• Search your firm's email domain in breach corpora. If a junior once signed up for a service with a work email and that service was later breached, the junior's password hash — and the fact of their working at your firm — is in an aggregated corpus. Rotate. Enforce a password manager. Turn on breach-alerting.
section.subtitle: Your client fingerprint
section.p: • A client is a signature too. A firm that publishes "we are proud to work with X" ties every future engagement to the reputational surface of X. Some clients require public listing; most do not. Default to not listing.

• Watch your invoicing metadata. A PDF invoice generated from your template carries the same metadata every time. If a client sends your invoice on to their auditor, the auditor now has your Created and Modified timestamps, your PDF producer version, and possibly the internal /CreationDate string. Flatten before sending.

• Watch your engagement letter defaults. A clause you used verbatim on ten engagements is a search-fingerprint. If one engagement letter leaks (litigation, discovery, a disgruntled junior), it can be tied to nine others via clause fingerprinting. Rotate boilerplate every year.
section.subtitle: Your tooling fingerprint
section.p: • The tools you use are a signature. If your curl requests always carry the same user-agent, an adversary logging their web-server access logs can spot you across every engagement. Rotate. Use standard, boring user-agents. Do not identify yourself in the string.

• Your scan-index accounts are a signature. Shodan and Censys keep query history per account. If your account credentials leak, every subject you ever pivoted on is inside the leak. Use per-engagement account credentials where scale permits, or accept the risk explicitly.

• Your archive-service accounts are a signature. Wayback and archive.today log capture requests against IP; a captured URL is a public record; a pattern of captures from your IP is not. Route captures through the archive services' native flow, not through your own scraper wearing your identity.
section.subtitle: Your peer network
section.p: • The people you talk to are a signature. A junior you trained who moved to a competitor is walking your method to the other side of the market. That is fine — it is how the profession renews — but the case files they took mental notes on are their working memory too. Do not confuse a peer with a friend.

• Public references between professionals in this field are visible. A LinkedIn endorsement, a shared talk, a co-authored paper. Each one ties you together in a way an adversary will map. If the working relationship needs to be quiet, keep it quiet from Day 1; there is no way to make it quiet later.
• Your mentor and your students are visible. Learn to read your own professional graph. If the graph would surprise the subject of your next engagement, that is a signal to think.
section.subtitle: Your operational hygiene
section.p: • Case-specific email aliases. Every engagement gets its own inbox alias — engagement-2026-041@yourdomain.com. When the engagement closes, retire the alias. A single career-long inbox is a discoverable time-line of every client you have ever had.
• Case-specific browser profiles. New Firefox / Brave / Chromium profile per engagement. Delete on close. Do not carry cookies from Engagement 041 into Engagement 042.

• Case-specific VMs where the frame requires it. For engagements with adversarial subjects, a fresh VM (Whonix, a tails-style workstation, or an ephemeral cloud desktop) per engagement. Destroy on close.
• Personal browser separate from work browser separate from research browser. Not a preference. A hygiene rule. See Volume 1.
section.subtitle: The habits you have already built, still hold
section.p: • Password manager, 2FA, encrypted disks, contact-syncing off. Volume 1. Volume 2. Volume 3. Same rules; more consequential now.
• Compartmentalise. Every identity you spin up for research eventually rots; retire it before it rots publicly.
section.subtitle: When someone is looking at you
section.p: If you know or suspect you have become a subject — a client's opposing counsel briefed to dig, a disgruntled subject who identified you by name, a state-level actor with an interest in your caseload — do not run this checklist on your normal accounts. The pattern of sudden hardening is itself a signal to a watcher. Move everything at once, from a clean device, in one session, or step back and ask a safeguarding professional for help. There is no shame in it.
section.subtitle: The line
section.p: You will not close every hole. You do not need to. What you need is enough friction that a casual adversary quits, and enough discipline that a serious one has to work — and that when a serious one is working on you, you notice before the finding lands with counsel on a Friday morning.
Read every chapter of this book as your own defensive manual. Close what you can. Live with what you cannot. Get back to the work.

p.emphasis: Every term this four-volume course uses more than once. Flip to it any time.

section.p: • Adverse action — under FCRA and its equivalents, a decision by an employer (not to hire, to withdraw an offer, to terminate) based on information in a consumer or investigative report. The employer must follow a specific notification and dispute process before and after the decision. The investigator does not run adverse action; the client does.
• AdSense ID / pub-id — Google's publisher identifier, pub-1234567890123456. Same pub-id across two sites = same wallet is being paid = strong attribution.
• Anchor — the one fixed known thing an investigation starts from. A domain, a photo, a handle, a phone number.
• Artefact — a captured, hashed, provenance-tagged piece of evidence in the case file. Not "a screenshot"; a screenshot plus its metadata plus its hash plus its log entry.
• Attribution — the third move in the loop: turning "this belongs to some person" into "this belongs to that person".
• Autonomous System (AS) — a chunk of the internet under one operator's routing control, e.g. AS13335. Groups IPs by who actually runs them.
• Banner — the short string a service emits on connection: version numbers, software names, sometimes hostnames.
• Breach data — a public dump of user records from a compromised platform. Evidence that an account existed; never a credential to log in with.
• Capture time — the timestamp of when a snapshot was taken (not when you are reading it). Every archived page, scan, or screenshot has one. Cite it.
• Case file — the ordered, retention-scheduled folder that holds one engagement's evidence, notes, drafts, correspondence, and provenance log.
• Certificate Transparency (CT) — the public append-only log where every trusted TLS certificate is recorded. Killed the idea that a hostname could stay secret.
• Chain of custody — the unbroken, documented record of an artefact's handling from capture to court. Chapter 3 of Volume 4 covers the shape.
• Chronolocation — dating an image from what is in the frame — sun angle, foliage, signage, snow.
• clientTransferProhibited — an EPP status code that stops a domain being transferred without unlocking. An anti-hijack lock, nothing more.
• CNAME — a DNS record pointing one hostname at another. Follow the chain; the alias target often reveals the tenant.
• Confidence ladder — the four rungs this course grades signals on: weak, moderate, strong, confirmed. Confirmed = self-link or hard identifier only.
• Confidence line — the sentence under each finding in a report that names the rung and the number of independent signals under it.
• Composite disclaimer — the sentence at the head of an illustrative case declaring that names, firms, and identifiers are fictional and any resemblance to real ones is coincidental.
• Counter-OSINT — the discipline of defending a footprint against exactly the methods this course teaches. Volume 4 Chapter 6.
• Counsel — the client's lawyer, retained or in-house. The person who reads your report and decides what it means legally. The person you call before you take on a borderline scope.
• Decision-grade report — the deliverable a working investigation produces: an artefact that survives a five-minute reading arc by counsel and enables a decision. Volume 4 Chapter 4.
• DKIM — a DNS-published cryptographic signature system that proves mail was sent by an authorised sender. s1._domainkey TXT records.
• DMARC — a DNS policy record telling receiving mail servers what to do when SPF/DKIM checks fail. Published at _dmarc.example.com.
• DNS — the phonebook that turns hostnames into IP addresses.
• DoH / DoT — DNS-over-HTTPS and DNS-over-TLS. Encrypted lookups. Research-hygiene concern, not query concern.
• DPA (national) — a national Data Protection Authority (the UK's ICO, France's CNIL, Germany's BfDI). The enforcement side of GDPR.
• DPIA — Data Protection Impact Assessment. A written record documenting how a processing activity (an investigation) meets the frame's proportionality requirement.
• Dork — a search-engine query built from operators — site:, inurl:, filetype:, intitle:.
• EEOC — the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; the frame for protected-class categories that never appear in a pre-hire report.
• Engagement letter — the written instrument that turns a favour into an engagement. Names the scope, the deliverable, the fee, the frame. Volume 4 Chapter 2.
• EXIF — the metadata block inside a photo file. Strip it before publishing; read it before drawing conclusions.
• Exposure — the first move in the loop: a trace already sitting in the open.
• Favicon — the small icon a browser shows in a site's tab. Reused across a subject's properties more often than they realise.
• Favicon hash — a MurmurHash3 of the favicon's raw bytes, base64-encoded. Scan indexes let you search by it.
• FCRA — the US Fair Credit Reporting Act. The frame under which most US pre-hire vetting is conducted, and which mandates the adverse-action process.
• Findings ladder — see confidence ladder.
• Fingerprint — a repeatable identifier derived from a configuration. Same setup, same fingerprint, across different IPs and hostnames.
• FOAF (friend-of-a-friend) — a technique that walks through other people's networks to reach the subject.
• GA4 — Google Analytics 4 measurement ID, shaped G-XXXXXXXX.
• GDPR — the EU General Data Protection Regulation. The frame that decides most European scope questions, and the reason WHOIS records went dark in 2018.
• Geolocation — identifying where an image was taken from what is visible in it.
• Hash chain — a JSONL log in which each line carries the SHA-256 of the previous line, making tampering detectable. The shape of a provenance log.
• Historical WHOIS — snapshots of WHOIS records from before the current one, often from before GDPR redaction.
• Hop / pivot — the second move in the loop: turning one trace into the next.
• HTTP header — the metadata sent with an HTTP request or response — Server, Set-Cookie, X-Powered-By.
• ICANN — the non-profit body that governs domain-name policy.
• Independence (of signals) — two signals only count as two votes if they came from separate sources. Three pages of the same leak is one signal, not three.
• Insider risk — an investigation targeting an existing employee flagged internally. A specific vetting frame with tighter procedural constraints than pre-hire.
• JARM — a 62-character TLS-stack fingerprint. Same JARM = same stack, same configuration.
• JA3 / JA4 / JA4S — client-side (JA3, JA4) and server-side (JA4S) TLS fingerprint formats.
• Leak — a dump of data made public. Treat as evidence, cite the source and date, never republish raw records.
• Legitimate interest (GDPR Art. 6(1)(f)) — one of the six lawful bases for processing personal data under GDPR; the one most investigation engagements rely on. Requires a documented balancing test.

• Limitations section — the part of a report that names what was outside scope, what could not be confirmed, and what a competent counter-investigator would have closed. What counsel reads to know how much weight to give the report.
• MurmurHash3 — a fast non-cryptographic hash function. Used by scan indexes for favicon fingerprinting.
• MX record — the DNS record naming a domain's mail server.
• Nameserver (NS) — the DNS server holding a domain's records.
• NDA — Non-Disclosure Agreement. The confidentiality instrument that covers material a client, a subject, or a partner firm shares in confidence.

• Notice / consent — where the frame requires it, a written notification to the subject that an investigation is being conducted, and their consent to it. Pre-hire vetting under FCRA requires notice and consent before the investigation begins.

• Partner firm — another firm you refer to for capabilities you do not offer — physical surveillance, forensic imaging, a jurisdiction you do not cover. Named in the engagement letter or a written amendment.
• Passive DNS (pDNS) — an archive of historical DNS resolutions collected by public resolvers.
• Peer read — a professional gate, not a favour. A same-seniority colleague reads the draft against a checklist with a mandate to say the uncomfortable sentence. Volume 4 Chapter 8.
• Phenology — the seasonal cycle of plants. In an outdoor photo, narrows the capture window to a few weeks.
• Pipeline — a small automation pipeline for investigation work, in the shape INPUT → NORMALISE → ENRICH → RANK → OUTPUT/REVIEW. Not a script — a shape. Volume 4 Chapter 7.
• Precertificate — a version of a TLS certificate submitted to CT logs before the final leaf is signed. What makes CT-based subdomain discovery near-real-time.
• Provenance — where a piece of evidence came from and how it reached you. Every claim in a report carries its provenance.
• Provenance log — the hash-chained JSONL record of every artefact in the case file: URL, capture time, tool, path, SHA-256, prev-line hash.
• Punycode / ACE form — the ASCII encoding DNS uses for internationalised domain names, prefixed xn--.
• Ranking (on the ladder) — the act of assigning weak, moderate, strong, or confirmed to a signal before writing it up.
• Redaction (WHOIS) — the post-GDPR practice of hiding registrant details behind placeholder text or a privacy-service alias.
• Registrar vs Registry — the registrar is the vendor you buy the domain from; the registry runs the TLD itself.

• Report anatomy — the five-section shape of a decision-grade report: scope recap, summary with confidence lines, findings in detail with inline provenance, what was ruled out, limitations. Volume 4 Chapter 4.
• Research browser — the clean profile with no cookies, no sync, no extensions you did not choose. Never confused with the working browser.
• Retainer — a deposit paid on execution of an engagement letter, held against future fees. Not a fee for services — a deposit.
• Reverse-IP / reverse-DNS — "what other hostnames resolved to this IP" vs. "what hostname does this IP claim in a PTR record".
• RFC 6962 — the specification defining Certificate Transparency logs.
• robots.txt — a text file at /robots.txt where a site politely asks crawlers to stay out. Advisory. The paths it names are often the most interesting.
• Ruled-out section — the part of a report naming the counter-explanations the investigator actively tested and killed. Where falsification is visible. The section counsel reads second.
• SAN (Subject Alternative Name) — the list of hostnames a single TLS certificate is valid for.
• Scan index — a searchable catalogue of every host visible on the public internet — Shodan, Censys, FOFA, ZoomEye.
• Scope — what the engagement letter authorises the investigator to look at, look for, and report on. The clause that turns curiosity into work.
• Scope creep — the drift by which an engagement expands beyond what the letter authorised. Requires a written scope amendment, or a stop-work memo.
• Scope amendment — a written change to an engagement's scope, signed by both parties. Verbal changes do not exist for scope.
• SCT (Signed Certificate Timestamp) — a receipt from a CT log, embedded in the cert itself.
• Self-link — a first-party assertion of ownership. The subject's own website linking to the handle. Strongest signal on the ladder.
• Silent rot — the failure mode where automation continues to return output but the output no longer reflects the source. Dashboards stay green; findings become stale. Volume 4 Chapter 7.
• Smoke test — a small daily check that a pipeline is producing plausible output. Instrumentation, not correctness.
• Snapshot — a saved copy of a page at a specific moment. Wayback, archive.today, your own SingleFile capture.
• Snapshot ID — an identifier for a snapshot in a case file, e.g. arch-2026-08-11-1943Z-9a2f. Cited inline in the report.
• Sock account — a clean investigative identity separate from the researcher's real one. Also called a research account.
• SPF — a DNS TXT record listing which mail servers are allowed to send as a domain.
• Stop-work memo — a written notice to counsel that continuing the engagement is not possible inside the frame or the scope. Followed by a refund of the unused retainer.
• Subdomain — a name to the left of the base domain.
• Subject — the person the investigation is about. Volume 4 uses subject rather than target deliberately — the vocabulary of a working professional.
• TLD — top-level domain. The last label of a hostname.
• TLS / SSL — the cryptographic layer under HTTPS. TLS is the current name.
• Tool decay diary — a paragraph a week noting what tool broke, what data-shape changed, what pivot went silent. Two months of that beats a year of after-the-fact panic.
• TXT record — a free-form DNS record. Holds SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and every SaaS verification token.
• UA-ID (legacy Google Analytics) — the older Google Analytics identifier, UA-XXXXX-Y. Deprecated in 2023 but still visible in archives.
• UTC timestamp — the timezone every timestamp in a report is stated in. Local timezones do not appear in decision-grade work.
• Vetting engagement — an investigation whose purpose is to answer a specific integrity or identity question — pre-hire, executive protection, insider risk, board/investor. Volume 4 Chapter 5.
• Verification token — a random string a third-party service asks a domain owner to publish in DNS to prove ownership.
• Wayback Machine — the Internet Archive's web history service at web.archive.org. Default first stop.
• WHOIS — the public record of who registered a domain, when, through which registrar, until when.
• Wildcard cert — a TLS certificate whose SAN is *.example.com.
• Working browser vs research browser — everyday Chrome signed into real accounts vs. clean profile with no cookies. Never confused.
